ana-mic-sa-j-80.why: Elastic laminae in the thick arterial media stretch during ventricular ejection. The wall then recoils passively during diastole, maintaining forward blood flow as ventricular ejection pauses.

notes.A: A large elastic artery such as the aorta has a thick media adapted to pulsatile pressure.
notes.B: Concentric sheets of fenestrated elastin stretch during systole and spring back during diastole.
notes.C: Smooth muscle cells between the elastic laminae help maintain the extracellular matrix of the media.
notes.D: Valves occur in many peripheral veins. Elastic arteries have no series of valves along their course.
notes.E: Diastolic forward flow is driven by release of stored elastic energy. It does not require active arterial contraction.

ana-mic-sa-d-124.why: Lymphatics return excess interstitial fluid and carry dietary lipids from the gut. Lymphoid tissues filter lymph, expose antigens to immune cells, and support lymphocyte development or expansion.

notes.A: Lymph nodes trap material arriving from tissues and bring lymph-borne antigens into contact with lymphocytes.
notes.B: Intestinal lacteals take up chylomicrons, and lymphatic drainage carries cellular debris away from tissues.
notes.C: Blind-ended lymphatic capillaries collect excess interstitial fluid for return to the venous circulation.
notes.D: Lymphocytes develop in primary lymphoid organs and proliferate after activation in secondary lymphoid organs.

ana-mic-sa-j-17.why: Afferent lymphatics deliver lymph to the subcapsular sinus at the convex surface. Lymph then passes through cortical and medullary sinuses and exits at the hilum.

notes.A: Nodes filter lymph, while the spleen filters blood. One or more efferent lymphatics leave a node at its hilum.
notes.B: Afferent lymphatics pierce the convex capsule and empty into the subcapsular sinus, also called the marginal sinus.
notes.C: Medullary cords contain lymphoid cells and plasma cells. They alternate with sinuses that carry lymph towards the hilum.

ana-mic-sa-j-18.why: The thymic medulla has relatively sparse thymocytes among epithelial reticular cells. Concentric layers of those epithelial cells form Hassall’s corpuscles, a distinctive feature of the medulla.

notes.A: Hassall’s corpuscles are medullary, but the normal thymus lacks the follicles and germinal centres seen in secondary lymphoid organs.
notes.B: A central arteriole within white pulp and a marginal zone are characteristic features of the spleen.
notes.C: Venous sinusoids and the cords of Billroth belong to the splenic red pulp.
notes.D: Concentric whorls of epithelial reticular cells form Hassall’s corpuscles within the thymic medulla.
notes.E: Maturing T cells are dispersed among epithelial reticular cells, giving the medulla a paler appearance than the cortex.

ana-mic-sa-j-19.why: The thymus has dark, thymocyte-rich cortices around paler medullary regions that are continuous between lobules. It supports T-cell maturation, and its functional parenchyma declines after puberty.

notes.A: Thymocyte precursors arrive through blood vessels. The thymic parenchyma lacks afferent lymphatics and normal lymphoid follicles.
notes.B: Closely packed immature thymocytes stain the cortex dark. The medulla has fewer lymphocytes and stains more lightly.
notes.C: Septa from the capsule divide the cortex into partial lobules while leaving the medulla continuous.
notes.D: Bone marrow precursors mature into T cells in the thymus. After puberty its lymphoid tissue is progressively replaced by fat.
notes.E: Cortical epithelial reticular cells enclose perivascular connective tissue and contribute to the blood–thymus barrier.

ana-mic-sa-j-21.why: Splenic white pulp mounts responses to blood-borne antigens. Blood passes through the red pulp, where macrophages screen cells and deformable erythrocytes can enter venous sinuses.

notes.A: White pulp has B-cell follicles like nodal follicles and periarteriolar T-cell sheaths functionally comparable to the nodal paracortex.
notes.B: Branched venous sinuses have a lining of elongated endothelial cells separated by narrow slits.
notes.C: Red pulp contains venous sinuses and the intervening cords of Billroth. In the open circulation, blood passes through the cords before entering the sinuses.
notes.D: Both red pulp and nodal medulla have cords between sinuses. Splenic sinuses carry blood, and nodal sinuses carry lymph.
notes.E: Splenic cords contain a mesh of reticular cells and fibres with macrophages that remove ageing erythrocytes.

ana-mic-sa-j-22.why: Phagocytes in the marginal zone and red pulp remove foreign material from blood. The narrow slits of the venous sinuses chiefly select for red cells able to deform.

notes.A: The spleen is the largest single lymphoid organ. Its white pulp forms lymphoid tissue around central arterioles.
notes.B: Ageing and damaged erythrocytes can be retained in the red pulp and removed by macrophages.
notes.C: White pulp lymphocytes proliferate after activation and mount adaptive responses to antigens arriving in blood.
notes.D: Reticular fibres support the splenic cords, where macrophages and antibody-secreting plasma cells can be found.

ana-mic-sa-j-23.why: Lymphocyte numbers increase during development in primary lymphoid organs and during immune responses in secondary organs. Filtration and stromal structure vary with the organ’s role.

notes.A: Lymph nodes have afferent vessels that carry lymph into them. The spleen and thymus lack this incoming route.
notes.B: Developing lymphocytes proliferate in primary organs. In secondary organs, mature lymphocytes proliferate in response to antigen.
notes.C: Splenic red pulp macrophages remove ageing erythrocytes. Other lymphoid organs do not share this role as a defining function.
notes.D: The spleen screens blood directly, whereas lymph nodes principally sample lymph arriving from peripheral tissues.
notes.E: The thymic parenchyma uses an epithelial reticular scaffold. Lymph nodes and spleen have reticular fibre frameworks.

ana-mic-sa-j-29.why: Duodenal submucosa contains Brunner’s glands, which release alkaline mucus to protect the mucosa from incoming gastric acid. Jejunal sections lack these submucosal glands.

notes.A: Large aggregated Peyer’s patches are characteristic of the ileum, so their absence cannot distinguish jejunum from duodenum.
notes.B: Intestinal crypts are present in the mucosa of both the duodenum and jejunum and renew the epithelium in each.
notes.C: The jejunum has particularly prominent circular folds, which increase the area of mucosa available for absorption.
notes.E: Chief cells produce pepsinogen in gastric glands and are absent from both these small intestinal segments.

ana-mic-sa-j-3.why: Conchae increase the mucosal surface in contact with inspired air and redirect it through narrow meatuses. Respiratory mucosa conditions the air, and olfactory mucosa occupies more superior patches.

notes.A: Each lateral nasal wall usually has superior, middle and inferior conchae along its height.
notes.B: The inferior concha is covered mainly by respiratory epithelium and helps warm and humidify inspired air.
notes.C: Much of the conchal surface has respiratory lining, but olfactory epithelium occupies part of the superior conchal region.
notes.D: The shelves increase nasal surface area and redirect airflow, bringing it close to the vascular, mucus-lined mucosa.
notes.E: Narrow meatuses guide streams of air close to the mucus layer, where particles can be trapped.

ana-mic-sa-j-4.why: The paranasal sinuses are air spaces within the frontal, ethmoid, sphenoid and maxillary bones. Their thin respiratory lining clears mucus through small openings into the nasal cavity.

notes.A: The spaces lie in bones surrounding the nasal cavity and are normally filled with air.
notes.B: The frontal, ethmoid, sphenoid and maxillary bones contain the named sinuses. The palatine and lacrimal bones do not.
notes.C: Sinus lining is generally thinner than nasal respiratory mucosa and has relatively few mucus-secreting goblet cells.
notes.D: Each sinus communicates with the nasal cavity through an ostium that permits ventilation and mucus drainage.

ana-mic-sa-j-5.why: The pharynx is a fibromuscular passage shared by air and food. Its lining changes from respiratory epithelium in much of the nasopharynx to abrasion-resistant squamous epithelium lower down.

notes.A: Its partially open anterior wall communicates with the nasal cavity, oral cavity and larynx. Inferiorly it continues into the oesophagus.
notes.B: The pharynx conducts air and food and modifies voice resonance through its shape and size.
notes.C: Pharyngeal lymphoid tissue includes diffuse lymphocytes and organised follicles, particularly in the tonsils.
notes.D: Ciliated respiratory epithelium covers much of the nasopharynx. Non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium protects surfaces exposed to food.
notes.E: Each auditory tube connects the lateral nasopharynx to the middle ear and allows pressure equalisation across the tympanic membrane.

ana-mic-sa-j-6.why: The larynx conducts air, produces voice and closes to protect the lower airway. Its cartilaginous framework and fibroelastic membranes are moved by intrinsic skeletal muscles.

notes.A: The larynx provides a conducting airway and produces sound. Closure at several levels helps protect the trachea during swallowing.
notes.B: The larynx is in the conducting portion. Gas exchange begins distally in respiratory bronchioles with alveoli in their walls.
notes.C: The thyroid and cricoid are hyaline cartilage. The leaf-shaped epiglottis is supported by elastic cartilage.
notes.D: Most arytenoid cartilage is hyaline. The corniculates, cuneiforms and portions of the arytenoids contain elastic cartilage.
notes.E: Fibroelastic membranes support the laryngeal folds, and intrinsic muscles change vocal fold position or tension.

ana-mic-sa-j-8.why: Intrapulmonary bronchi maintain respiratory epithelium and submucosal glands. Irregular cartilage plates replace the tracheal rings, and a smooth muscle layer deep to the mucosa regulates airway calibre.

notes.A: Intrapulmonary bronchi retain a respiratory lining but have cartilage plates and a circumferential muscle layer rather than the tracheal arrangement.
notes.B: Bronchi conduct air towards the gas-exchange regions. Their mucociliary surface clears particles and their mucosa helps warm the air.
notes.C: Smooth muscle with elastic fibres lies around the lamina propria, superficial to the submucosa and its glands.

ana-mic-sa-j-54.why: Respiratory bronchioles are the first airways with alveoli opening out of their walls. The bronchiolar segments still have cuboidal epithelium and smooth muscle, while the alveoli permit gas exchange.

notes.A: Alveolar openings interrupt the bronchiolar wall, providing the first sites for gas exchange along the airway.
notes.B: Cuboidal cells and club cells line the airway segments, with ciliated cells most evident proximally. Alveoli have thin squamous lining cells.
notes.C: Smooth muscle and elastic fibres persist in the wall segments between adjacent alveolar openings.
notes.D: Respiratory bronchioles follow terminal bronchioles and lead into alveolar ducts with more extensive alveolar openings.
notes.E: Thin type I pneumocytes line most of the surface of each alveolar outpocketing and shorten the diffusion distance.

ana-mic-sa-j-56.why: Type II pneumocytes secrete surfactant at the alveolar air–liquid interface. It lowers surface tension as alveoli get smaller in expiration, improving compliance and resisting collapse.

notes.A: Surfactant spreads as a thin surface film at the air-facing boundary of the alveolar lining fluid.
notes.B: Surface-active phospholipids reduce cohesive forces at the air–liquid interface and lower alveolar surface tension.
notes.C: Without adequate surfactant, surface tension increases the tendency of small alveoli to collapse during expiration.
notes.D: Insufficient surfactant in premature infants contributes to low lung compliance and neonatal respiratory distress syndrome.
notes.E: Cuboidal type II pneumocytes store surfactant in lamellar bodies and release it onto the alveolar surface.

ana-mic-sa-j-57.why: The thinnest alveolar septum has fused epithelial and endothelial basal laminae that minimise the gas diffusion distance. Thicker regions contain interstitial connective tissue and can accommodate more tissue fluid.

notes.A: The septum includes alveolar epithelium and capillary endothelium with their basal laminae. These laminae are fused at the thinnest sites.
notes.B: Fibroblasts, macrophages, collagen and elastic fibres are found in the interstitial part of the septum.
notes.C: The thin route crosses lining fluid and surfactant, a type I pneumocyte, the fused basal laminae and capillary endothelium.
notes.D: The thicker regions have connective tissue and cells between the separate epithelial and endothelial basal laminae.
notes.E: The thin side has the shortest diffusion path. Interstitial fluid can collect in the thicker connective tissue compartment.

ana-mic-sa-j-58.why: Alveolar macrophages patrol the air spaces and septal connective tissue. They engulf inhaled particles and microbes and remove erythrocytes that leak into alveolar tissue or air spaces.

notes.A: These phagocytes clear particulates from air spaces and can remove extravasated erythrocytes from the septum.
notes.B: Macrophages occur both within the alveolar lumen and in connective tissue of the alveolar septum.
notes.C: Some pigment-bearing macrophages remain in the septal interstitium for years, especially if the particles are indigestible.
notes.D: Inhaled carbon can remain visible as dark pigment inside macrophages, including in tissue from smokers.
notes.E: Alveolar macrophages can engulf inhaled mycobacteria. Phagocytosis alone does not guarantee that the organisms are killed.

ana-mic-sa-j-2.why: Olfactory mucosa contains receptor neurons with supporting and basal cells. Serous secretion from Bowman’s glands dissolves odorants and clears them from the sensory surface.

notes.A: Pigment in the olfactory mucosa gives the region its characteristic yellowish to yellow-brown appearance.
notes.B: The pseudostratified olfactory lining contains receptor neurons, sustentacular cells and basal cells. Goblet cells characterise adjacent respiratory epithelium.
notes.C: Serous secretion from Bowman’s glands dissolves odorants and helps wash previously bound stimuli away.
notes.D: Bundles of olfactory receptor axons run through the lamina propria beside the glands and towards the cribriform plate.
notes.E: Basal progenitor cells can differentiate into new bipolar olfactory receptor neurons after birth.

ana-mic-sa-j-25.why: Interlacing skeletal muscle allows the tongue to change shape during speech and swallowing. Its dorsal papillae have different functions, and the ventral mucosa is smooth.

notes.A: Lingual papillae are on the dorsum. The ventral surface has thin, smooth lining mucosa.
notes.B: Muscle bundles cross in different planes, allowing the tongue to change shape as well as position.
notes.C: Keratin makes filiform tips appear whitish. Vessels show through the thinner epithelium of fungiform papillae, giving a reddish appearance.
notes.D: Minor salivary glands lie among muscle bundles. Their ducts release secretions onto the tongue surface.
notes.E: Filiform papillae provide friction for handling food and lack the taste buds found in the other papillary types.

ana-mic-sa-j-26.why: Gastric chief cells release pepsinogen, while parietal cells provide acid and intrinsic factor. Gastric pits collect gland secretions, and a bicarbonate-rich mucus barrier protects the mucosal surface.

notes.A: Chief cells release inactive pepsinogen. Acid activates it in the lumen, and intrinsic factor is secreted by parietal cells.
notes.B: Surface mucous cells produce mucus and bicarbonate, which help protect the epithelium from acid and pepsin.
notes.C: A gastric pit is a surface invagination into which several mucosal glands can empty.
notes.D: Parietal cells secrete hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor. G cells release gastrin and chief cells release pepsinogen.
notes.E: Rugae consist of mucosa and submucosa. They flatten when the stomach distends after a meal.

ana-mic-sa-j-28.why: The jejunum typically has taller circular folds and longer vasa recta. Greater mesenteric fat, more arterial arcades and aggregated lymphoid nodules favour ileum, particularly distally.

notes.A: The jejunum typically has a wider lumen and thicker wall with taller, more closely spaced circular folds.
notes.B: The proximal jejunum has fewer tiers of arcades and longer vasa recta. Ileal arcades have more tiers and shorter straight vessels.
notes.C: Ileal villi are generally shorter and often blunter than those of the jejunum.
notes.D: Goblet cell density generally increases distally. Ileal mesenteric fat often extends to the bowel margin and obscures the vessels.
notes.E: Aggregated lymphoid nodules called Peyer’s patches are particularly prominent in the distal ileum.

ana-mic-sa-j-30.why: The proximal duodenal bulb usually has a smooth outline because prominent circular folds are absent there. Distally, barium outlines folds of mucosa and submucosa.

notes.B: Lymphoid nodules are immune tissue and do not produce the repeated transverse contrast pattern of circular folds.
notes.C: This reverses the distribution. The proximal bulb is smooth and the circular folds become prominent farther along the duodenum.
notes.D: Villi are microscopic mucosal projections throughout the duodenum, including the bulb. Larger circular folds account for this contrast pattern.
notes.E: A muscularis externa is present throughout the duodenum. The contrast outlines folds projecting from the inner mucosa and submucosa.

ana-mic-sa-j-31.why: Portal venous and hepatic arterial blood mix in sinusoids and flow toward central veins. Bile travels in the opposite direction through canaliculi toward ducts in portal tracts.

notes.A: Blood from both sources mixes in sinusoids. Fenestrated endothelium allows plasma solutes to reach hepatocytes through the space of Disse.
notes.B: Sinusoidal blood flows from the lobular periphery toward the central vein, which serves as the outlet.
notes.C: Central veins drain into larger collecting veins that join the hepatic veins, which empty into the inferior vena cava.
notes.D: Fenestrated sinusoidal endothelial cells form a discontinuous barrier, and Kupffer macrophages lie on its luminal side.
notes.E: Membranes of adjacent hepatocytes enclose the bile canaliculus. Tight junctions separate bile from the surrounding intercellular space.

ana-mic-sa-j-61.why: The listed gut organs share a thin muscularis mucosae at the base of the mucosa and a myenteric plexus deeper between muscle layers of the muscularis externa.

notes.A: The uterus, uterine tube and vas deferens contain smooth muscle, but they do not have the gut’s muscularis mucosae and enteric plexus.
notes.B: The duodenum contains both structures. The ureter, tongue and epididymis lack this combination of gut wall features.
notes.C: The oesophagus has both. The ureter, ejaculatory ducts and trachea lack the characteristic myenteric plexus.
notes.E: The gallbladder lacks a distinct muscularis mucosae, and the urinary and genital structures lack the gut’s paired arrangement.

ana-mic-sa-j-62.why: Orbicularis oris provides a skeletal muscle core within the lips. Contraction changes lip shape and helps seal the oral opening during suckling, chewing and speech.

notes.A: During suckling the lips form a seal that helps maintain the negative pressure needed to draw milk into the mouth.
notes.B: The lips shape vowels and come together for bilabial speech sounds such as those beginning the words ‘pat’ and ‘bat’.
notes.C: Lip closure helps retain food in the oral cavity while the tongue and cheeks move it during chewing.
notes.E: Lips and cheeks both have external skin and internal oral mucosa with skeletal muscle between the surfaces.

ana-mic-smd-147-p9.why: A glomerulus is a tuft of fenestrated capillaries within Bowman’s capsule. Blood enters through an afferent arteriole, and an efferent arteriole carries it away after filtration.

notes.A: Renal arterial branches deliver blood upstream. The glomerular tuft itself has capillary walls adapted for filtration.
notes.B: Renal veins collect blood downstream of the kidney’s capillary beds. The tuft drains directly into an efferent arteriole.
notes.C: Venules receive blood after it has traversed downstream capillary beds. They do not make up the tuft inside Bowman’s capsule.
notes.E: Afferent and efferent arterioles lie at the vascular pole. The network between them is formed by capillaries.

ana-mic-smd-173-p15.why: Arcuate arteries curve along the bases of the renal pyramids at the corticomedullary junction. They give rise to cortical radiate arteries that ascend into the cortex.

notes.A: A lobar vessel supplies a renal lobe. The curved arteries at the pyramid bases are the arcuate branches.
notes.C: Interlobar arteries run in the renal columns between pyramids and give off arcuate arteries near the pyramid bases.
notes.D: Cortical radiate arteries branch from arcuate arteries and pass outward through the cortex, giving off afferent arterioles.
notes.E: Segmental arteries branch near the renal hilum to supply renal segments. They lie upstream of the arcuate arteries.

ana-mic-smd-174-p15.why: Glomerular capillaries lie between two arterioles. The efferent arteriole carries blood away and helps maintain the capillary hydrostatic pressure needed for filtration into Bowman’s space.

notes.A: Many capillaries have a basement membrane. In the glomerulus it is a specialised layer of the filtration barrier.
notes.B: The barrier allows water and small solutes through readily. It restricts cells and most large plasma proteins.
notes.D: Glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure is greater than in many systemic capillary beds, favouring the formation of filtrate.
notes.E: Glomerular capillaries are fenestrated and have a continuous basement membrane. They are distinct from hepatic or splenic sinusoids.

ana-mic-mic19-47-p12.why: Filtrate crosses fenestrated capillary endothelium, the shared glomerular basement membrane and the slit diaphragms between podocyte foot processes before entering Bowman’s urinary space.

notes.B: The macula densa is part of the distal tubule at the vascular pole and lies outside the filtration barrier.
notes.C: Podocytes form the visceral epithelium of Bowman’s capsule. The distal tubular macula densa is separate from the capillary filtration surface.
notes.D: Extraglomerular mesangial cells and the macula densa are at the vascular pole. They are components of the juxtaglomerular apparatus.
notes.E: Intraglomerular mesangial cells support the tuft between capillary loops. They are absent from the normal three-layer filtration pathway.

ana-mic-mic19-73-p19.why: Vasopressin promotes aquaporin-2 insertion in collecting duct cells. When the hormone is absent, water reabsorption falls, producing persistent passage of large volumes of dilute urine.

notes.A: Excess vasopressin increases collecting duct water permeability and favours water retention with relatively concentrated urine.
notes.C: Haematuria is the presence of red cells in urine. It does not account for persistently high volumes of dilute urine.
notes.D: Aldosterone promotes distal sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion. It does not replace vasopressin’s control of water permeability.
notes.E: Afferent arteriolar dilation can raise glomerular filtration, but urine concentration still depends on collecting duct water handling.

ana-mic-sa-j-36.why: Parallel tubular segments, collecting ducts and vasa recta give the renal medulla a striated appearance. Renal corpuscles and convoluted tubules lie in the cortex.

notes.A: The medulla is arranged as renal pyramids. Eight to twelve is a teaching estimate and the actual number varies.
notes.B: Straight tubular segments including the loops of Henle, collecting ducts and vasa recta run in parallel within the medulla.
notes.C: Convoluted proximal and distal tubules lie in the cortex. The medullary segments run mainly in straight, parallel courses.
notes.D: Medullary rays are bundles of straight tubules and ducts that project into the cortex, where the convoluted tubules also lie.
notes.E: Podocytes and filtration slits are in cortical renal corpuscles. The macula densa is adjacent to their vascular pole.

ana-mic-sa-j-38.why: The renal corpuscle comprises the glomerular capillary tuft and Bowman’s capsule. Its visceral podocytes and capillary endothelium share a basement membrane at the filtration surface.

notes.A: Slit diaphragms bridge filtration slits between adjacent podocyte foot processes and help restrict macromolecules.
notes.B: Mesangial cells and the filtration barrier are within the corpuscle. The macula densa is an adjacent distal tubular structure.
notes.C: Podocyte and endothelial basal laminae contribute to the shared glomerular basement membrane.
notes.D: Bowman’s capsule has an outer parietal epithelium and visceral podocytes over the tuft, whose capillaries have fenestrated endothelium.

ana-mic-sa-j-41.why: The bladder stores urine behind a distensible urothelium. Interlacing detrusor smooth muscle empties the reservoir, and a single smooth triangular trigone lies at its base.

notes.A: The detrusor is conventionally described as three smooth muscle layers, although the bundles interlace and the layers are often indistinct.
notes.B: The bladder expands as urine accumulates. Its urothelium accommodates stretching while maintaining a barrier to urine.
notes.C: There is one trigone, bounded by the two ureteric openings and the internal urethral opening.
notes.D: The bladder has urothelium over a connective tissue layer and detrusor. Secretory alveoli are not a defining bladder feature.

ana-mic-sa-j-42.why: The prostatic urethra receives prostatic ducts, the membranous part passes through the striated urethral sphincter, and the spongy part runs within the corpus spongiosum.

notes.A: Prostatic ducts open into the prostatic urethra, particularly into grooves beside the urethral crest.
notes.B: The external urethral sphincter surrounds the membranous part, which commonly has pseudostratified or stratified columnar epithelium.
notes.C: The spongy urethra is about fifteen centimetres long. Bulbourethral ducts open into its proximal portion.
notes.D: The spongy part is mostly lined by pseudostratified or stratified columnar epithelium, with more distal squamous lining.

ana-mic-sa-j-64.why: The macula densa is a cluster of closely packed distal tubular cells at the glomerular vascular pole. It senses luminal sodium chloride and signals to adjust filtration and renin release.

notes.A: The macula densa lies at the vascular pole. Its signals help coordinate tubuloglomerular feedback and renin release.
notes.B: It senses sodium chloride in tubular fluid at the vascular pole. The urinary pole is where filtrate enters the proximal tubule.
notes.C: It lies at the end of the thick ascending limb near the distal convoluted tubule and has a sensing role.
notes.D: Reduced luminal sodium chloride promotes signals that stimulate renin secretion by adjacent granular juxtaglomerular cells.
notes.E: Tall, closely spaced cells produce a dense group of nuclei where the distal tubular segment abuts the vascular pole.

ana-mic-sa-j-65.why: Juxtaglomerular cells are modified smooth muscle cells, mainly in the afferent arteriolar wall near the vascular pole. They have rounded nuclei and store renin in granules.

notes.A: Granular cells are in arteriolar walls. The macula densa is the neighbouring specialised distal tubular epithelium.
notes.B: Juxtaglomerular cells release renin. Renal erythropoietin is produced mainly by interstitial cells near peritubular capillaries.
notes.C: The afferent arteriolar media near the glomerulus contains specialised smooth muscle cells with a secretory function.
notes.D: Compared with contractile smooth muscle cells, granular cells have rounder nuclei and cytoplasmic renin granules.

ana-mic-sa-j-66.why: The kidney releases erythropoietin in response to reduced oxygen availability. Erythropoietin stimulates red cell production in the bone marrow, while renin helps regulate effective circulating volume.

notes.A: Glomerular filtration and tubular secretion help eliminate many foreign compounds and their metabolites into urine.
notes.B: Adjusting urinary water excretion, including responses to vasopressin, helps regulate total body water.
notes.C: The kidneys regulate sodium excretion and therefore help control extracellular fluid volume over time.
notes.D: Renin initiates the angiotensin cascade, influencing sodium retention, vascular tone and effective circulating volume.

ana-mic-sa-j-67.why: Medullary rays are radial bundles within the cortex. They contain straight tubular segments and collecting ducts, while renal corpuscles and convoluted tubules occupy the surrounding cortical labyrinth.

notes.A: The rays belong to the cortex. Renal columns are separate extensions of cortex between medullary pyramids.
notes.B: Renal corpuscles and convoluted tubules lie in the cortical labyrinth. The rays are formed from straight structures.
notes.C: The rays have straight tubular portions, but renal corpuscles are outside them and papillary ducts open at the papilla.
notes.D: Renal corpuscles lie in the cortical labyrinth. Their presence distinguishes it from the medullary rays.
notes.E: Each ray contains parallel straight portions of nephrons and collecting ducts running between cortex and medulla.

ana-mic-sa-j-69.why: The renal cortex includes a labyrinth of renal corpuscles and convoluted tubules, interspersed with medullary rays containing straight tubular segments and collecting ducts. Calyces occupy the renal sinus.

notes.A: Cortical labyrinth contains renal corpuscles and convoluted proximal and distal tubules. Straight tubular segments are also present in cortical rays.
notes.B: The collecting ducts merge into papillary ducts near the medullary apex. Papillary ducts are outside the cortex.
notes.C: In addition to corpuscles and medullary rays, the cortex contains abundant proximal and distal convoluted tubules.
notes.D: Minor calyces receive urine at the papillae and lie in the renal sinus, outside the cortical tissue.

ana-mic-smd-97-p1.why: A deficiency of vasopressin release from the posterior pituitary causes central diabetes insipidus. Collecting ducts reabsorb less water, leading to large volumes of dilute urine.

notes.A: Diabetes mellitus can cause polyuria through glucose-driven osmotic diuresis. The stem describes a deficiency of vasopressin.
notes.C: Diabetic ketoacidosis involves insulin deficiency and accumulation of ketone bodies. It does not describe impaired vasopressin secretion.
notes.D: Coma is a state of impaired consciousness. It does not identify the endocrine cause of dilute polyuria.
notes.E: Polydipsia describes increased thirst and can follow urinary water loss. It does not name the condition caused by low vasopressin.

ana-mic-smd-99-p1.why: The parietal layer of Bowman’s capsule is simple squamous epithelium. Visceral podocytes cover the glomerular capillaries, and the capsule continues into the proximal tubule at the urinary pole.

notes.B: The glomerulus is a capillary tuft inside Bowman’s capsule. The proximal convoluted tubule begins at the urinary pole.
notes.C: Podocytes are branching epithelial cells that cover glomerular capillaries. They do not line the nephron’s tubules.
notes.D: Filtration slits lie between podocyte foot processes. Endothelial fenestrations are separate openings in the capillary lining.
notes.E: The proximal tubule is lined by specialised cuboidal cells. Podocytes form the covering of the glomerular tuft.

ana-mic-smd-100-p2.why: The juxtaglomerular apparatus includes distal tubular macula densa cells, arteriolar granular cells and extraglomerular mesangial cells. Podocytes cover glomerular capillaries and help form the filtration barrier.

notes.A: Granular cells store and release renin and are found mainly in the afferent arteriolar wall near the vascular pole.
notes.B: The macula densa senses tubular sodium chloride and signals to neighbouring cells at the vascular pole.
notes.D: Extraglomerular mesangial cells lie between the distal tubule and the glomerular arterioles and form part of the apparatus.
notes.E: Lacis cells are another name for extraglomerular mesangial cells, a component of the juxtaglomerular apparatus.

ana-mic-smd-132-p5.why: The urinary system forms, transports, stores and expels urine through the kidneys, ureters, bladder and urethra. The rectum is a terminal portion of the digestive tract.

notes.A: The kidneys filter plasma and adjust the filtrate to produce urine, so they are urinary organs.
notes.B: The bladder stores urine delivered by the ureters and empties it into the urethra during voiding.
notes.D: The ureter carries urine from the renal pelvis to the urinary bladder by smooth muscle peristalsis.
notes.E: The urethra carries urine from the bladder to the exterior and is the final urinary passage.

ana-mic-smd-135-p6.why: Renal pyramids are conical medullary regions containing parallel tubules and ducts. The base faces the cortex, and the tip forms a papilla projecting into a minor calyx.

notes.B: Renal columns are extensions of cortical tissue between neighbouring medullary pyramids rather than the conical medullary structures.
notes.C: The renal pelvis is the funnel-shaped common collecting space in the sinus that continues into the ureter.
notes.D: Nephrons are microscopic filtration and tubular units. Many of their tubular segments contribute to each pyramid.
notes.E: Calyces are collecting spaces that receive urine from the papillae. They are separate from the medullary tissue.

ana-mic-smd-136-p6.why: The renal pelvis is the funnel-shaped expansion continuous with the proximal ureter. It collects urine from the major calyces and channels it into the ureter.

notes.A: The renal sinus is a cavity containing calyces, the renal pelvis, vessels and fat. It is larger than the collecting lumen.
notes.C: A major calyx joins multiple minor calyces and carries urine into the pelvis upstream of the ureter.
notes.D: A minor calyx is a small cup that receives urine at a renal papilla and empties into a major calyx.
notes.E: The renal corpuscle is the microscopic filtration unit formed by glomerular capillaries and Bowman’s capsule.

ana-mic-smd-138-p7.why: The glomerular filtration barrier restricts most circulating albumin, and the proximal tubule retrieves much of the small amount that passes. Eliminating excess albumin is not a normal renal regulatory function.

notes.A: Kidneys adjust water excretion in response to changes in body water and vasopressin, helping maintain osmolality.
notes.B: Renal tubular reabsorption and secretion help control the concentrations of electrolytes such as sodium and potassium.
notes.D: The kidneys make erythropoietin in response to reduced oxygen availability. It stimulates bone marrow red cell production.
notes.E: Regulation of sodium and water balance, together with renin release, helps control arterial blood pressure.

ana-mic-smd-139-p7.why: At the urinary pole of Bowman’s capsule, filtrate enters the proximal convoluted tubule. Its brush border provides surface area for the first stage of bulk reabsorption.

notes.A: The nephron loop receives filtrate after it has passed through the proximal convoluted and straight tubular segments.
notes.C: The distal convoluted tubule receives fluid after it has passed through the loop of Henle.
notes.D: The collecting duct receives tubular fluid after passage through the distal nephron and connecting segment.
notes.E: A minor calyx receives urine from papillary ducts, after the filtrate has traversed the nephron and collecting system.

ana-mic-smd-140-p7.why: The distal convoluted tubule is the last nephron segment listed before the collecting system. Its outflow passes through a short connecting tubule to reach a collecting duct.

notes.A: The nephron loop returns fluid to the cortex and leads to the distal convoluted tubule upstream of the collecting system.
notes.B: The proximal convoluted tubule begins at Bowman’s capsule and leads to the straight proximal segment.
notes.D: A papillary duct receives fluid downstream from converging collecting ducts and opens at the papilla.
notes.E: The minor calyx receives urine from papillary ducts after it has left the microscopic collecting system.

ana-mic-smd-142-p8.why: The proximal convoluted tubule reabsorbs most filtered sodium and water, along with nearly all filtered glucose and amino acids at normal plasma concentrations. Its brush border increases transport area.

notes.A: Filtration occurs across the glomerular barrier. The proximal tubule receives the filtrate after it enters Bowman’s space.
notes.C: The proximal tubule contributes to acid handling and produces ammonium, but bulk reabsorption accounts for most of its transport.
notes.D: Proximal tubular cells secrete some drugs into the lumen. This is a secondary role alongside large-volume reabsorption.
notes.E: The proximal tubule reabsorbs water in bulk, and collecting duct water permeability provides the main final adjustment of urine volume.

ana-mic-smd-8-p8.why: Renal arterial branches lead from interlobar to arcuate and cortical radiate vessels. An afferent arteriole supplies each glomerulus, and its efferent arteriole feeds a downstream capillary bed.

notes.A: Branches proceed from interlobar to arcuate to cortical radiate arteries. Cortical radiate arteries therefore come after the arcuate branches.
notes.C: The afferent arteriole carries blood into the glomerular capillaries. The efferent arteriole carries it away.
notes.D: Cortical radiate arteries arise from arcuate arteries, and the afferent arteriole is upstream of the glomerulus.
notes.E: Interlobar arteries give rise to arcuate arteries at the pyramid bases. Cortical radiate branches follow from there.

ana-mic-smd-145-p9.why: Water and small solutes cross fenestrated endothelium, the shared glomerular basement membrane and slit diaphragms between podocyte processes. Together these layers limit the passage of blood cells and large proteins.

notes.A: Foot processes and the slits between them are components of the podocyte layer. Endothelium and basement membrane are also required.
notes.B: Mesangial matrix supports capillary loops within the tuft. It is separate from the basement membrane on the filtration path.
notes.D: The fenestrations are in the glomerular capillary endothelium. The parietal wall of Bowman’s capsule is outside the barrier.
notes.E: The visceral podocytes form the epithelial layer of the barrier. The parietal layer and mesangium are not serial filtration layers.

ana-mic-smd-149-p10.why: Strong renal sympathetic stimulation constricts renal arterioles, reducing renal blood flow and usually lowering filtration. It also promotes renin release through beta-1 receptors on granular cells.

notes.A: Sympathetic alpha-adrenergic signalling constricts afferent arterioles, particularly when activation is strong.
notes.C: Beta-1 stimulation of juxtaglomerular granular cells promotes renin release as part of the volume-preserving response.
notes.D: A marked fall in renal perfusion can produce ischaemia when sympathetic vasoconstriction is severe.
notes.E: Increased filtration is the exception. The additional claim about renin release describes an established sympathetic response.

ana-mic-smd-153-p11.why: The loop of Henle multiplies an osmotic gradient along the medulla. Salt transport in the ascending limb helps build that gradient, allowing vasopressin-sensitive collecting ducts to conserve water.

notes.A: Countercurrent multiplication does occur, and the single mechanism leaves out the resulting gradient and ability to concentrate urine.
notes.B: The loop does increase interstitial sodium chloride, but this describes only the salt-gradient part of its role.
notes.C: The medullary gradient helps support hypertonic urine when ducts are water permeable. This is one consequence of the mechanism.
notes.E: Both effects are valid, and the combination leaves out countercurrent multiplication that establishes the gradient.

ana-mic-smd-155-p11.why: The ureter and bladder are lined by urothelium, also called transitional epithelium. Its superficial umbrella cells flatten with distension and maintain a barrier against urine.

notes.A: Stratified squamous epithelium protects surfaces such as the distal urethral opening. The ureter and bladder have specialised urothelium.
notes.B: Pseudostratified columnar epithelium can occur in the urethra. The ureter and bladder lining has multiple layers with umbrella cells.
notes.C: Simple cuboidal epithelium lines many renal tubules. The ureter and bladder require a stretchable stratified lining.
notes.E: Simple columnar epithelium lines much of the gut. Urothelium has several layers adapted to distension.

ana-mic-smd-156-p11.why: The detrusor is the smooth muscle coat of the bladder. When it contracts during micturition, it raises intravesical pressure as outlet resistance falls, expelling urine.

notes.A: Smooth muscle in the ureter wall generates peristalsis. The detrusor is located in the bladder wall.
notes.C: Smooth muscle at the bladder neck helps control the outlet. The detrusor provides the pressure for bladder emptying.
notes.D: The external urethral sphincter is striated muscle. Detrusor smooth muscle contracts involuntarily during voiding.
notes.E: The renal pelvis has its own smooth muscle to help propel urine. Detrusor is the muscle coat of the bladder.

ana-mic-smd-167-p14.why: Glomerulonephritis involves inflammation or immune-mediated injury of glomeruli. Damage to their filtration barrier can allow blood or protein into urine, and filtration rate can fall.

notes.B: A floating kidney is an abnormally mobile kidney, also called nephroptosis. It is not a primary glomerular inflammatory disorder.
notes.C: Polycystic kidney disease produces numerous fluid-filled cysts, which distort renal tissue as they enlarge.
notes.D: Pyelonephrosis is a term for disease of the renal pelvis and kidney. Inflammation centred on the glomeruli is glomerulonephritis.
notes.E: Kidney stones are concretions within the urinary tract. They can obstruct urine flow but do not define glomerular inflammation.

ana-mic-smd-168-p14.why: At rest the kidneys receive roughly one-fifth of cardiac output, about 1 to 1.2 litres of blood per minute in a typical adult. This flow supports filtration and solute regulation.

notes.B: Two litres per minute would represent nearly half of a typical resting cardiac output, above the usual renal share.
notes.C: Three litres per minute would account for most resting cardiac output. The kidneys normally receive about one-fifth.
notes.D: Four litres per minute approaches the total resting cardiac output of a small adult and exceeds typical renal blood flow.
notes.E: Five litres per minute is close to typical total resting cardiac output. The kidneys receive only a fraction of it.

ana-mic-smd-169-p14.why: Vasopressin activates V2 receptors on collecting duct principal cells, increasing apical aquaporin-2 channels. The higher water permeability lets water leave tubular fluid along the medullary osmotic gradient.

notes.A: A fall in vasopressin reduces apical aquaporin-2 abundance and decreases collecting duct water reabsorption.
notes.C: Aldosterone chiefly stimulates sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion. Vasopressin is the direct regulator of apical aquaporin-2 insertion.
notes.D: A fall in plasma osmolality normally suppresses vasopressin release, reducing collecting duct water permeability.
notes.E: ACTH acts mainly on the adrenal cortex to stimulate glucocorticoid production. It does not directly insert collecting duct water channels.

ana-mic-smd-175-p15.why: In water-permeable portions of the thin descending limb, water moves into the hyperosmotic medullary interstitium. This leaves progressively more concentrated tubular fluid on the way down.

notes.A: Much of the thin descending limb has high water permeability. The ascending limb has low water permeability.
notes.B: Solute permeability varies with the segment. The characteristic response in water-permeable descending segments is osmotic water loss.
notes.C: The more concentrated medullary interstitium draws water out of the descending limb by osmosis.
notes.E: Net water movement out of the tubule raises luminal concentration as fluid descends through the medulla.

ana-mic-mic19-23-p6.why: The ureter wall consists of a urothelial mucosa, smooth muscle muscularis and outer adventitia. The muscularis propels urine by peristalsis, and the adventitia anchors the ureter to adjacent tissue.

notes.B: The ureter is largely retroperitoneal, with an outer connective tissue adventitia. It is separate from the visceral peritoneum.
notes.C: Urothelium lines the lumen, and endothelium is found in vessels supplying the wall.
notes.D: The smooth muscle coat is one part of the wall. The ureter also has a mucosa and an adventitia.
notes.E: In the upper ureter, muscle is generally inner longitudinal and outer circular. An outer longitudinal layer is added distally.

ana-mic-mic19-24-p7.why: The male urethra is a shared outlet for urine and semen during separate physiological processes. Closure at the bladder neck during ejaculation helps direct semen outward.

notes.B: The urethra serves both systems, but ejaculation and urinary voiding are normally coordinated as distinct events.
notes.C: The male urethra passes through the prostate, pelvic outlet and penis, making it longer than the female urethra.
notes.D: The same urethral channel carries urine during voiding and semen during ejaculation.
notes.E: Much of the male urethra has pseudostratified or stratified columnar lining, with urothelium proximally and squamous epithelium distally.

ana-mic-mic19-25-p7.why: Creatinine passes through the glomerular filter and a small amount is secreted by proximal tubular cells. Negligible reabsorption distinguishes it from sodium, potassium, glucose and water.

notes.A: Proximal sodium transport reabsorbs a large fraction of the filtered sodium load and helps drive solute and water reabsorption.
notes.B: A substantial fraction of filtered potassium is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule, largely via the paracellular pathway.
notes.C: Sodium-glucose cotransport reabsorbs almost all filtered glucose at normal plasma concentrations.
notes.E: Water follows solutes osmotically, so the proximal tubule reabsorbs much of the filtered water.

ana-mic-mic19-31-p9.why: Renal columns are bands of cortical tissue between neighbouring medullary pyramids. Interlobar vessels pass through these columns towards the base of each pyramid at the corticomedullary junction.

notes.A: The renal sinus is an internal cavity at the hilum. A renal column is solid cortical tissue between pyramids.
notes.B: The renal pelvis is the expanded proximal end of the ureter and receives urine from major calyces.
notes.C: A nephron is a functional unit made of a renal corpuscle and tubule. A column is a larger anatomical region.
notes.E: The conical structures in the medulla are renal pyramids. Cortical columns extend into the spaces between pyramids.

ana-mic-mic19-32-p9.why: Several minor calyces usually unite to form each major calyx. The major calyces drain into the renal pelvis, which funnels urine toward the proximal ureter.

notes.B: A nephron has a renal corpuscle and a tubular portion. Its terminal tubular fluid reaches a collecting duct.
notes.C: The renal cortex and medulla are the main tissue regions. Calyces are parts of the urine collecting system.
notes.D: Renal pyramids are cones of medullary tissue. They discharge urine into calyces through ducts opening at the papillae.
notes.E: The terminal tip of a renal pyramid is the papilla, which projects into a minor calyx.

ana-mic-mic19-36-p10.why: The loop of Henle establishes the medullary osmotic gradient. With vasopressin, the collecting ducts become water permeable and use this gradient to produce urine more concentrated than plasma.

notes.A: Bulk water and solute reabsorption takes place in the proximal tubule, where tubular fluid is normally close to plasma osmolality.
notes.B: The distal convoluted tubule reabsorbs salt and helps dilute tubular fluid. Final water recovery occurs mainly farther downstream.
notes.C: The collecting duct is where vasopressin increases water recovery. This relies on a gradient built in part by the loop.
notes.D: The loop establishes the gradient, but the collecting duct must be water permeable for the final urine to concentrate.

ana-mic-mic19-42-p11.why: Proximal convoluted tubule cells have a tall apical brush border, folded basolateral surfaces and abundant mitochondria. These adaptations provide membrane area and energy for high rates of reabsorption.

notes.A: Podocytes have branching foot processes and slit diaphragms for filtration. They do not have a tall absorptive brush border.
notes.C: Thin limb cells form a flat simple squamous lining with far less cytoplasm than proximal tubular cells.
notes.D: Distal tubular cells can have substantial basolateral folding but lack the tall, dense proximal brush border.
notes.E: The distal convoluted tubule has shorter and sparser apical microvilli, so its lumen looks clearer in sections.

ana-mic-mic19-43-p11.why: Both the parietal layer of Bowman’s capsule and the thin limb of Henle have flattened simple squamous cells. Thick tubular segments generally have simple cuboidal epithelium.

notes.A: Both convoluted tubules have simple cuboidal epithelium. The proximal one has a more prominent brush border.
notes.C: The visceral layer has podocytes, but the thick descending portion is the cuboidal proximal straight tubule.
notes.D: Proximal convoluted tubules and smaller collecting tubules have cuboidal cells. Larger collecting ducts become more columnar.
notes.E: The thick ascending limb and smaller collecting tubules generally have cuboidal lining, although their cells differ in function.

ana-mic-mic19-44-p11.why: Ureteric urothelium stretches as urine passes. Its superficial umbrella cells, tight junctions and surface plaques maintain a high-resistance barrier to water and solute movement.

notes.A: Surface plaques and tight junctions provide the main barrier. Mucus secretion is not the defining role of ureteric urothelium.
notes.B: Urothelium is the lining of both the ureter and bladder, where it combines distensibility with low permeability.
notes.C: Stones can injure the lining. The usual role of urothelium is to provide a flexible barrier to urine.
notes.D: Reabsorption is a function of renal tubular epithelium. The ureter transports urine without substantially changing its composition.

ana-mic-mic19-46-p12.why: Collecting tubules vary their water permeability in response to vasopressin. When permeability increases, water leaves into the hyperosmotic medulla and the remaining fluid becomes more concentrated.

notes.A: Collecting tubules can secrete ions, but filtration occurs in glomerular capillaries upstream in the nephron.
notes.B: The collecting system helps concentrate urine, while filtration takes place separately across the glomerular barrier.
notes.D: Collecting tubules regulate water and ion handling. They do not have a mucous lining for lubrication.
notes.E: Stretchable urothelium lines structures such as the ureter and bladder, whereas collecting tubules have cells specialised for transport.

ana-mic-mic19-50-p13.why: Major calyces empty into the renal pelvis, the funnel-shaped collecting lumen within the renal sinus. The pelvis narrows as it becomes continuous with the ureter.

notes.A: A papilla is the tip of a renal pyramid. Papillary ducts release urine into the surrounding minor calyx.
notes.C: The renal medulla is parenchyma containing tubules and collecting ducts. It is not the hollow collector that receives the calyces.
notes.D: The renal cortex contains corpuscles and tubules. The collecting cavity described lies centrally within the sinus.
notes.E: The sinus contains the pelvis, calyces, vessels and fat. Only the lumen of the pelvis receives urine from major calyces.

ana-mic-mic19-53-p14.why: Ageing can reduce functional nephron number, glomerular filtration and maximum urine concentrating ability. The older kidney’s concentrating response to vasopressin is often blunted, even when hormone secretion is preserved.

notes.A: Functional nephron number can fall with age because of nephron loss and increasing glomerulosclerosis.
notes.B: Measured glomerular filtration commonly falls with age, although the rate and extent vary between individuals.
notes.D: Age-related changes in bladder sensation, neural control or detrusor function can alter the voiding reflex.
notes.E: Urethral closure pressure and sphincter function can decline with age, contributing to urinary leakage in some people.

ana-mic-mic19-60-p15.why: Collecting ducts converge to form papillary ducts of Bellini. These ducts open at the tip of a renal pyramid, where a minor calyx receives the urine.

notes.A: The loop of Henle passes tubular fluid to the distal nephron before it enters the collecting system.
notes.B: The distal convoluted tubule delivers fluid toward the connecting tubule and collecting duct, upstream of papillary drainage.
notes.D: Plasma filtration occurs in the renal corpuscle, and the filtrate first passes into the proximal tubule.
notes.E: The ureter carries urine from the renal pelvis to the bladder, downstream of both minor and major calyces.

ana-mic-mic19-61-p16.why: Plasma filtration occurs in the renal corpuscle. Hydrostatic pressure drives water and small solutes across glomerular capillary walls and podocyte slit diaphragms into Bowman’s space.

notes.A: The loop of Henle has tubular segments that transport water and solutes after the filtrate has already formed.
notes.B: The distal convoluted tubule adjusts electrolyte content by transport across its epithelium. It receives existing filtrate.
notes.C: A papillary duct carries the final tubular fluid to a minor calyx. It is downstream of the filtration site.
notes.E: The ureter transports urine to the bladder by peristalsis. Its urothelium forms a barrier and has no plasma filtration role.

ana-mic-mic19-62-p16.why: The kidneys vary sodium, water, acid and electrolyte excretion to maintain the internal environment. Volume control and the renin–angiotensin system also help regulate arterial pressure.

notes.A: The kidneys adjust sodium and water excretion to help maintain the extracellular fluid and circulating blood volumes.
notes.B: Net acid excretion and bicarbonate reclamation help keep blood pH within its normal range.
notes.C: Renal sodium handling and renin release influence circulating volume and vascular tone, respectively helping regulate arterial pressure.
notes.D: Variable tubular transport helps keep plasma concentrations of sodium, potassium and other ions within physiological limits.

ana-mic-mic19-65-p17.why: Renal failure is a loss of kidney function severe enough to impair waste excretion and control of fluid, electrolytes or acid–base balance. It can develop acutely or chronically.

notes.A: Glomerulonephritis is a cause of glomerular injury that can impair filtration. The stem describes the resulting functional state generally.
notes.B: Polycystic kidney disease causes expanding renal cysts and can eventually reduce function. It describes a specific cause.
notes.C: Calculi are urinary stones. They can obstruct flow and damage renal function but are not the general functional diagnosis.
notes.E: Haematuria refers to blood in urine and can occur even when overall excretory function is preserved.

ana-mic-mic19-66-p17.why: An adult filters roughly 180 litres of fluid per day but typically excretes only about one to two litres. Net tubular reabsorption therefore returns roughly 99 percent to the circulation.

notes.A: One percent is approximately the fraction of filtered water normally excreted, leaving almost all to be reabsorbed.
notes.B: If only 38 percent were recovered, most of the filtered water would be lost. Normal daily urine volume is far lower.
notes.C: This is near the fraction that may be reabsorbed in the proximal tubule alone. Further reabsorption occurs downstream.
notes.D: Recovery continues after the proximal tubule. Reabsorbing only about three-quarters overall would leave far more than a normal urine volume.

ana-mic-mic19-67-p17.why: Collecting ducts empty through papillary ducts into the calyces, which drain into the renal pelvis. The ureter then carries urine to the bladder and the urethra carries it outside.

notes.A: The ureter carries urine from the renal pelvis to the bladder. The urethra is the final passage after the bladder.
notes.B: The collecting ducts reach the calyces before the renal pelvis. The bladder receives urine through the ureters.
notes.D: The collecting duct is upstream of the renal pelvis. The urethra is the final outlet downstream of the bladder.
notes.E: The renal pelvis drains into the ureter. From there urine passes to the bladder and then through the urethra.

ana-mic-mic19-68-p17.why: Renal corpuscles all lie in the cortex, including those near the corticomedullary junction. The medulla contains tubular and vascular structures such as loops, collecting ducts and vasa recta.

notes.A: Vasa recta are medullary capillaries derived from efferent arterioles of juxtamedullary nephrons, not sites containing glomeruli.
notes.B: Even juxtamedullary renal corpuscles are on the cortical side of the junction. Their long tubular loops descend into the medulla.
notes.D: The renal pelvis is the funnel-shaped lumen that receives urine from major calyces. It contains no renal corpuscles.
notes.E: Calyces are urine-collecting spaces around papillae and have a urothelial lining. The filtering tufts are within renal cortex.

ana-mic-mic19-74-p19.why: Urine leaves the renal pelvis through a ureter and enters the bladder for storage. During voiding it exits through the urethra to the exterior.

notes.A: The ureter passes out through the renal hilum and carries urine to the bladder. Its flow is toward the bladder.
notes.C: Glomerular filtration produces fluid entering Bowman’s space. It then passes through renal tubules before reaching the ureter.
notes.D: The urethra follows the bladder and carries urine outside. Urine approaches the bladder through the ureter.
notes.E: Minor calyces drain into major calyces and the pelvis. From the pelvis, the next passage is the ureter.

ana-mic-mic19-85-p22.why: A renal corpuscle comprises the glomerular capillary tuft and the surrounding Bowman’s capsule. The capsule collects filtered fluid and delivers it to the proximal tubule at the urinary pole.

notes.B: The descending limb is a tubular segment that receives filtrate after it has passed through the proximal tubule.
notes.C: A renal pyramid is a medullary region containing straight tubules, ducts and vessels. The corpuscle is microscopic and cortical.
notes.D: The papilla is the tip of a renal pyramid where the collecting system discharges urine into a minor calyx.
notes.E: Only the capillary tuft and its surrounding capsule form the corpuscle. The loop, pyramid and papilla are separate structures.

ana-mic-mic19-91-p23.why: Filling stretches the bladder wall and activates mechanosensitive afferents. Their signals reach sacral and higher centres, initiating the reflex that coordinates detrusor contraction and outlet relaxation.

notes.B: Motor output acts downstream of sensory signalling. It helps contract the detrusor and relax the external sphincter.
notes.C: Filling pressure relates to bladder distension, but the initiating sensory event is activation of wall stretch receptors.
notes.D: Sympathetic efferents mainly support urine storage. The voiding reflex begins with afferent signals from the bladder wall.
notes.E: Stretch supplies the initiating sensory signal. Motor neuron activity is part of the response after the signal reaches the cord.

ana-mic-mic19-93-p24.why: Macula densa cells detect changes in luminal sodium chloride at the end of the thick ascending limb. Their signals adjust afferent arteriolar tone and renin release.

notes.A: Aldosterone acts on cells of the distal nephron to regulate sodium reabsorption. The sensing role here concerns tubular sodium chloride.
notes.B: Vasopressin raises collecting duct water permeability. Macula densa cells monitor the sodium chloride content of tubular fluid.
notes.C: Pressure within the afferent arteriole can influence renin release through granular cells. The macula densa monitors luminal solute delivery.
notes.E: Macula densa cells are themselves specialised tubular epithelial cells. Their relevant stimulus is sodium chloride in the tubular lumen.

ana-mic-mic19-94-p24.why: Glomerular filtrate contains water and small dissolved solutes at concentrations close to the free plasma fractions. The filtration barrier holds back most plasma proteins, including most albumin.

notes.A: Glucose is small and freely filtered. It is normally reclaimed later by sodium-dependent transport in the proximal tubule.
notes.B: Small unbound hormones can pass through the filter. Protein binding or large molecular size limits filtration of other hormones.
notes.C: Small dissolved ions generally pass the glomerular filter. Tubular transport then adjusts their final urinary concentrations.
notes.E: The ionised and small complexed fractions of calcium can be filtered. Calcium bound to plasma protein is largely retained.

ana-mic-mic19-95-p24.why: Acute alcohol intake can suppress vasopressin release. Collecting ducts then reabsorb less water, so more dilute urine is passed while the reduction in vasopressin persists.

notes.A: The characteristic acute water diuresis is due to altered vasopressin release. It does not depend on alcohol remaining in the tubular lumen.
notes.B: An increase in filtration is not needed. Dilute urine results when less water is reabsorbed downstream in the collecting duct.
notes.C: Increased vasopressin would raise collecting duct water permeability. That favours water conservation rather than dilute urine.
notes.E: ACTH acts on the adrenal cortex. Collecting duct water permeability is controlled mainly by vasopressin in this response.

ana-mic-smd-131-p5.why: The kidneys regulate volume, pH and electrolyte composition and eliminate metabolic wastes. Most albumin remains in plasma, and proximal tubular retrieval limits normal urinary albumin loss.

notes.B: Renal control of water and sodium excretion helps preserve circulating blood volume over time.
notes.C: The kidneys reclaim bicarbonate and excrete acid as ammonium and titratable acid, helping stabilise blood pH.
notes.D: Filtration and tubular secretion help remove organic wastes, including urea and creatinine, in urine.
notes.E: The kidneys can change reabsorption or secretion of ions such as sodium and potassium to regulate their plasma concentrations.

ana-mic-smd-154-p11.why: A fall in vasopressin lowers water permeability in the collecting ducts. Less water is reabsorbed, increasing urine volume and decreasing urine osmolality when other factors are unchanged.

notes.A: Urine volume rises because less water leaves the collecting ducts. This is paired with a decrease in urine concentration.
notes.B: Lower water permeability leaves more water in the tubular lumen, so a fall in urine output is the opposite prediction.
notes.C: Urine osmolality falls as the remaining solutes are diluted. The volume of urine rises at the same time.
notes.E: The concentration change is in the right direction, but lower vasopressin increases urine volume rather than reducing it.

ana-mic-smd-148-p9.why: The glomerular barrier readily passes water and small solutes while strongly restricting proteins around the size of albumin or larger. A small amount of albumin can still be filtered.

notes.A: Sodium ions are far smaller than albumin and pass into the filtrate. Their final excretion depends on tubular transport.
notes.B: Glucose is a small freely filtered solute and is normally reclaimed by proximal tubular cells.
notes.D: Free amino acids pass through the filter and are then substantially reabsorbed by the proximal tubule.
notes.E: Urea is a small freely filtered waste product and is also transported in parts of the tubule.

ana-mic-smd-150-p10.why: Glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure drives plasma water and small solutes into Bowman’s space. Plasma oncotic pressure and hydrostatic pressure in Bowman’s space oppose that movement.

notes.A: Glomerular filtration occurs by pressure-driven bulk flow. Active transport is important later for handling solutes along the tubule.
notes.B: Plasma proteins generate colloid osmotic pressure that draws water into capillaries, opposing outward filtration.
notes.D: The kidney has no separate pump that pushes fluid across the glomerular barrier. The driving pressure comes from the circulation.
notes.E: Solvent drag describes solute carried with moving water. The hydrostatic pressure gradient drives the water movement first.

ana-mic-mic19-22-p6.why: Glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure supplies the main outward force for filtration. Barrier structure governs permeability, and retained plasma proteins provide an inward oncotic force.

notes.A: Podocyte shape and slit diaphragms influence what crosses. The driving force is a pressure difference across the barrier.
notes.B: The thin fenestrated endothelium provides a permeable surface. It does not generate the outward filtration pressure.
notes.D: The basement membrane helps determine which solutes can cross. Hydrostatic pressure provides the force moving fluid through it.
notes.E: The colloid osmotic pressure generated by plasma proteins draws water toward the capillaries and opposes net outward filtration.

ana-mic-mic19-92-p23.why: The glomerular filter consists of fenestrated capillary endothelium, a shared basement membrane and podocyte slit diaphragms. Renal fascia is a gross connective tissue sheath around the kidney.

notes.A: Fenestrated capillary endothelium forms the innermost layer that plasma encounters on the filtration path.
notes.B: Podocyte foot processes cover the abluminal side of the glomerular capillaries and form the final epithelial layer.
notes.D: The shared glomerular basement membrane lies between capillary endothelium and the podocyte foot processes.
notes.E: Slit diaphragms bridge the spaces between neighbouring podocyte foot processes and provide part of the filtration barrier.

ana-mic-sa-j-43.why: Spermatogenesis requires high intratesticular testosterone and support from Sertoli cells inside seminiferous tubules. Production may continue into older age, although its efficiency can decline.

notes.A: Leydig cells produce testosterone, which acts through androgen-responsive cells including Sertoli cells to support germ cell development.
notes.B: The seminiferous epithelium can remain active in older adults, although sperm output and quality may decline.
notes.C: Sertoli cells support developing germ cells, maintain their local environment and help coordinate maturation and release.

ana-mic-sa-j-44.why: Sertoli cells support germ cells within seminiferous tubules, respond to follicle-stimulating hormone and secrete androgen-binding protein. They also help form the blood–testis barrier and clear residual bodies.

notes.A: Sertoli cells express follicle-stimulating hormone receptors and respond by supporting the environment required for spermatogenesis.
notes.B: Sertoli cells make androgen-binding protein. Contraction of the peritubular wall is a function of surrounding myoid cells.
notes.C: The nurse-cell function is correct, but Sertoli cells lie within the seminiferous epithelium. Leydig cells occupy the interstitium.
notes.D: Sertoli cells phagocytose residual bodies. Dividing germ cells are generally more vulnerable than Sertoli cells to heat and irradiation.
notes.E: Large irregular Sertoli cells are found in seminiferous tubules and form the lining at the beginning of the straight tubules.

ana-mic-sa-j-45.why: Peritubular myoid cells are flattened, actin-rich cells around seminiferous tubules. Their contraction helps propel testicular fluid and released germ cells toward the rete testis.

notes.A: Actin microfilaments support contraction and help give peritubular myoid cells their smooth-muscle-like properties.
notes.B: The characteristic peritubular cells lie outside the epithelial basal lamina, in the connective tissue coat surrounding each tubule.
notes.C: The myoid cells encircle the seminiferous tubules as part of the peritubular wall.
notes.D: They are flattened contractile cells arranged in layers of the tunica propria outside the seminiferous epithelium.
notes.E: Contraction of the peritubular wall helps move testicular fluid and newly released sperm that have limited motility.

ana-mic-sa-j-46.why: Efferent ductules have a scalloped lumen formed by alternating tall ciliated and shorter absorptive epithelial cells. The ductules reclaim fluid and help transport sperm toward the epididymis.

notes.A: Tall ciliated cells alternate with shorter cells bearing absorptive microvilli, giving sections a characteristic scalloped outline.
notes.B: Long stereocilia are prominent on epididymal principal cells. Efferent ductules have true motile cilia on some cells.
notes.C: A thin smooth muscle layer surrounds the ductules and aids transport through the lumen.
notes.D: Their alternating epithelial heights differ from those of the epididymis, and their muscle coat is thinner than the vas deferens.
notes.E: Cilia and smooth muscle aid movement, while shorter cells absorb much of the testicular fluid.

ana-mic-sa-j-47.why: The epididymal epithelium absorbs fluid and modifies luminal contents as sperm mature. Smooth muscle helps move sperm along the duct, and the tail serves as the main storage region.

notes.A: The tail acts as a reservoir with relatively little spontaneous movement during storage. Stronger contractions move sperm during ejaculation.
notes.B: Principal cells have stereocilia. The general epithelial outline is more even than the scalloped lining of efferent ductules.
notes.C: Smooth muscle encircles the duct and becomes thicker toward the tail, contributing to transport.
notes.D: The epididymis absorbs fluid, clears cellular debris and supports sperm maturation. Its tail stores mature sperm.
notes.E: The epithelium modifies epididymal fluid by adding compounds such as glycerophosphocholine and glycoproteins.

ana-mic-sa-j-48.why: Seminal vesicles are folded secretory glands that contribute fructose-rich fluid to semen. Smooth muscle in their walls contracts during ejaculation, delivering secretions into the ejaculatory ducts.

notes.A: The secretions include fructose as an energy substrate for sperm, as well as prostaglandins and ascorbate.
notes.B: Both the seminal vesicle and terminal ampulla show a folded mucosa with a smooth muscle wall, though their glandular functions differ.
notes.C: Sperm mature and are stored mainly in the epididymis. The seminal vesicles provide fluid added during ejaculation.
notes.D: Secretions are expelled by smooth muscle in the gland wall, which is a muscular coat rather than a muscularis mucosae.

ana-mic-sa-j-49.why: The prostate is the largest male accessory gland. Its tubuloalveolar glands sit in fibromuscular stroma and secrete citrate, acid phosphatase and proteases that help liquefy semen.

notes.A: The prostate has abundant smooth muscle between its glands as part of its fibromuscular stroma.
notes.B: The prostate lies behind the pubic symphysis, but sperm mature and are stored in the epididymis.
notes.C: Prostatic secretion contains citrate, acid phosphatase and enzymes that break down the seminal coagulum after ejaculation.
notes.D: Eosinophilic smooth muscle lies between secretory glands. Rounded prostatic concretions may be seen within glandular lumina.

ana-mic-sa-j-50.why: Vasectomy interrupts sperm transport through the ductus deferens while preserving testosterone production and erectile function. Sperm already beyond the interruption can remain in ejaculates until cleared.

notes.A: Erection depends on neurovascular pathways and erectile tissue. These are separate from the interrupted sperm ducts.
notes.B: Libido, erection and ejaculation generally remain possible. Most ejaculate volume comes from accessory gland secretions.
notes.C: Residual sperm can persist for weeks or months, which is why post-vasectomy semen testing is used to confirm clearance.
notes.D: Testicular spermatogenesis can continue after the ducts are interrupted, including into older age.
notes.E: The procedure is intended to prevent sperm from reaching the ejaculate once post-vasectomy semen clearance is confirmed.

ana-mic-sa-j-51.why: The ductus deferens and seminal vesicle duct unite to form each ejaculatory duct. The duct traverses the prostate to deliver sperm and seminal vesicle fluid into the urethra.

notes.A: The intraprostatic passage lacks a distinct muscular coat of its own and lies within fibromuscular prostatic tissue.
notes.B: A layered muscular coat is characteristic of the ductus deferens. The ejaculatory duct lacks a separate two-layer muscle coat.
notes.C: Pseudostratified columnar epithelium can line the ejaculatory duct, with variation along the passage.
notes.D: Sperm arrive from the ductus deferens and pass through the ejaculatory duct with fluid from the seminal vesicle.
notes.E: Sertoli cells support germ cells in the seminiferous epithelium. They are absent from the ejaculatory duct lining.

ana-mic-sa-j-73.why: Spermatogenesis is temperature-sensitive. Countercurrent heat exchange in the spermatic cord helps cool incoming arterial blood, and sustained increases in testicular temperature can impair germ cell development.

notes.A: The pampiniform venous plexus carries relatively cooler blood around branches of the testicular artery, allowing heat exchange before arterial entry.
notes.B: Proliferating germ cells, especially dividing spermatogonia, are vulnerable to ionising radiation because DNA damage can interrupt cell division.
notes.C: An undescended abdominal testis remains at a higher temperature than a scrotal testis, which can impair the germinal epithelium over time.
notes.D: Repeated hot-water exposure can impair semen measures. Studies of tight clothing are less consistent, so this is a possible association.

ana-mic-sa-j-10.why: Endocervical glands remain intact during menstruation and change their mucus under hormonal influence. Mucus is thinner around ovulation, while obstruction of a gland opening can produce a retention cyst.

notes.A: The endocervix has deep branching mucus-secreting glands. Spiral arteries are characteristic of the functional endometrium of the uterine body.
notes.B: Endocervical secretion changes with the cycle, but its lining does not undergo menstrual shedding like the endometrial functional layer.
notes.C: Around ovulation, oestrogen promotes more abundant, less viscous mucus that sperm can traverse more readily.
notes.D: Progesterone favours thicker cervical mucus after ovulation, reducing receptivity to sperm passage.
notes.E: A blocked cervical gland opening can trap mucus and distend the gland, forming a Nabothian cyst.

ana-mic-sa-j-11.why: The growing uterus develops longer, larger myometrial cells and a greatly expanded blood supply. Early in pregnancy the corpus luteum supplies progesterone before the placenta assumes most production.

notes.A: Myometrial smooth muscle cells enlarge markedly in pregnancy. The stated lengths illustrate the approximate scale of hypertrophy.
notes.B: Uterine vascular growth and remodelling support the increased demands of the uterus and developing placenta.
notes.C: Early trophoblastic human chorionic gonadotrophin maintains the corpus luteum and its progesterone output until the placenta takes over.
notes.D: The corpus luteum can regress after the luteal–placental shift, but placental production of progesterone and oestrogens continues.

ana-mic-sa-j-13.why: Frequent suckling raises prolactin and suppresses hypothalamic reproductive signalling. Reduced pulsatile luteinising hormone delays ovulation, and ovarian cycles can resume as suckling becomes less frequent.

notes.A: Frequent suckling sustains prolactin release and contributes to the suppression of the reproductive axis during lactation.
notes.B: Elevated prolactin contributes to reduced pulsatile gonadotrophin-releasing hormone signalling and hence reduced luteinising hormone pulsatility.
notes.C: When suckling becomes less frequent, reproductive hormonal signalling can recover and ovulation may resume before the first bleed.
notes.D: The lactational amenorrhoea method requires absent menses, full or nearly full breastfeeding, and an infant younger than six months.

ana-mic-sa-j-14.why: Spiral arteries supply the endometrial functional layer and lengthen as it regenerates. After progesterone withdrawal, late-cycle vasoconstriction contributes to breakdown of this layer during menstruation.

notes.A: Spiral arteries serve the endometrium of the uterine body. The mucus-secreting endocervix does not have this cyclic arterial arrangement.
notes.B: Loss of luteal progesterone is associated with intermittent constriction of spiral arteries and breakdown of the functional layer.
notes.C: Spiral arteries rise from the basal region and supply the overlying stratum functionalis, which is shed during menstruation.
notes.D: After menstruation the functional layer regrows and its spiral arteries lengthen again from vessels retained in the basal layer.
notes.E: The vessels elongate and coil as the endometrium develops, becoming well developed in the secretory phase.

ana-mic-sa-j-15.why: Dense collagen-rich connective tissue makes up much of the cervical wall. Its matrix helps the cervix remain closed during pregnancy and remodel to permit dilatation during labour.

notes.A: The cervix has much less smooth muscle than the uterine body. A figure near fifteen percent is approximate and varies by region.
notes.B: Collagen-rich connective tissue, elastic fibres and smooth muscle are distributed unevenly through the cervical wall.
notes.C: The cervix controls access to the uterine cavity, then softens and dilates to allow passage of the fetus during labour.
notes.D: Collagen is the dominant component. Elastic fibres and a smaller smooth muscle component contribute to cervical mechanical properties.

ana-mic-sa-j-70.why: Granulosa lutein cells form when follicular granulosa cells luteinise after ovulation. These large, pale steroid-producing cells differ from the smaller theca lutein cells derived from theca interna.

notes.A: Granulosa lutein cells make up much of the corpus luteum and are prominent in routine histological sections.
notes.C: Abundant smooth endoplasmic reticulum is typical of steroid-producing cells and contributes to progesterone synthesis.
notes.D: Granulosa lutein cells are large and relatively pale, in part because their steroidogenic cytoplasm contains lipid droplets.
notes.E: Progesterone secreted by the corpus luteum acts on endometrial glands and stroma to maintain the secretory state.
