ana-mic-sa-j-71.why: Decidual cells develop from progesterone-responsive endometrial stromal cells. They release factors including prolactin and help regulate trophoblast invasion and maternal immune adaptation at the implantation site.

notes.A: Decidual cells arise from stromal fibroblast-like cells below the epithelium. They enlarge and change their secretory activity.
notes.B: Decidual prolactin is produced locally and is commonly used as a marker of endometrial stromal decidualisation.
notes.C: Decidual cells help regulate trophoblast depth and contribute to the local immune environment that supports implantation.

ana-mic-sa-j-75.why: The luteinising hormone surge promotes luteinisation after ovulation. Granulosa and theca interna cells form distinct steroid-producing populations within the yellow, lipid-rich corpus luteum.

notes.A: The corpus luteum develops from both granulosa cells and cells of the theca interna in the ruptured follicle.
notes.B: Granulosa lutein cells are generally larger and paler, while theca lutein cells are smaller and lie near connective tissue septa.
notes.C: Luteinising hormone promotes luteinisation after ovulation. Lipid-associated pigment contributes to the yellow appearance.
notes.D: Both lutein cell populations contain lipid and participate in steroid production. The corpus luteum secretes progesterone and oestrogens.

ana-mic-sa-j-76.why: Follicular atresia is degeneration rather than ovulation and can affect follicles at different developmental stages. In larger follicles, granulosa cells, the oocyte and the follicular basement membrane show characteristic changes.

notes.A: Atresia can occur at several stages, from early growing follicles to large antral follicles.
notes.B: Granulosa cells undergo apoptosis and lose their regular arrangement, particularly in atretic antral follicles.
notes.C: Thickening of the basement membrane between the granulosa and theca can produce the characteristic glassy membrane.
notes.D: The oocyte can disintegrate while its surrounding zona pellucida persists transiently as a collapsed remnant.
notes.E: Connective tissue may enter the degenerating follicle and replace its former cellular and fluid spaces.

ana-mic-sa-j-78.why: Uterine tube folds are most complex in the ampulla and decrease toward the uterus. Ciliated cells favour the distal region and oestrogen-dominant phase, while secretory cells are more prominent proximally.

notes.A: Tall, branching mucosal folds nearly fill the ampullary lumen. The isthmus and intramural segment have simpler folds.
notes.B: Ciliated epithelial cells are generally more prominent near the infundibulum, with more secretory cells toward the uterine end.
notes.C: The expected regional tendency is reversed here. Distal segments are usually more densely ciliated than proximal segments.
notes.D: Oestrogen during the follicular phase favours ciliation, while secretory activity becomes more prominent during the luteal phase.
notes.E: Oestrogen favours ciliogenesis. Progesterone has a greater role in luteal-phase secretory changes and can reduce ciliary activity.

ana-mic-sa-j-79.why: The superficial functional endometrium is shed at menstruation and regrows from retained basal tissue. Implantation usually occurs high in the uterine cavity near the fundus.

notes.A: The functional portion undergoes cyclic changes and is the layer lost during menstrual shedding.
notes.B: The basal layer remains against the myometrium and retains the deep portions of endometrial glands, which help regenerate the lining.
notes.C: Normal implantation favours the upper uterine cavity, often along an anterior or posterior wall in the fundal region.

ana-mic-sa-j-32.why: Thyroid follicular cells produce iodinated thyroglobulin and store it in luminal colloid. Parafollicular cells secrete calcitonin, while follicular thyroid hormones support development and regulate metabolic activity.

notes.A: Follicles are approximately spherical. Their simple lining is often cuboidal and can flatten when relatively inactive.
notes.B: Colloid contains thyroglobulin with iodinated residues from which active thyroid hormones are released after uptake and processing.
notes.C: Parafollicular cells occur at the base of follicular epithelium or between follicles and generally do not reach the colloid.
notes.D: Calcitonin from parafollicular cells can lower blood calcium in part by reducing osteoclast-mediated bone resorption.
notes.E: Thyroid hormones are important for fetal growth and nervous system development and help regulate energy expenditure after birth.

ana-mic-sa-j-33.why: The parathyroids usually lie along the posterior thyroid surface. Chief cells secrete parathyroid hormone to regulate calcium and phosphate, while oxyphil cells are larger and more intensely eosinophilic.

notes.A: The calcium and phosphate function is correct. The glands are usually on the posterior surface rather than embedded within thyroid parenchyma.
notes.B: Chief cells predominate and have central nuclei and relatively pale cytoplasm. Glycogen and lipid content varies with cell state.
notes.C: Oxyphil cells are larger and contain many mitochondria, which give the cytoplasm its strong eosinophilia.

ana-mic-sa-j-34.why: Pancreatic islets are ductless endocrine cell clusters closely associated with capillaries. Beta cells release insulin, alpha cells release glucagon and delta cells secrete somatostatin.

notes.A: Alpha and beta cells are two major populations among the endocrine cells of the islets.
notes.B: Beta cells release insulin to reduce blood glucose, while alpha cells release glucagon to increase it.
notes.C: Acini and ducts belong to the exocrine pancreas. Islet products enter the local capillary network.
notes.D: A rich network of capillaries provides a route for islet hormones to enter the circulation.
notes.E: Delta cells secrete somatostatin, which helps regulate hormone secretion within the islet.

ana-mic-sa-j-35.why: The adrenal cortex accounts for most of the gland and synthesises steroid hormones in three zones. The medulla contains chromaffin cells that release catecholamines.

notes.A: The medulla secretes catecholamines. The cortex produces steroids derived from cholesterol, rather than protein hormones.
notes.B: The cortex constitutes roughly nine-tenths of the gland and supplies mineralocorticoids, glucocorticoids and androgens.
notes.C: The three named zones are cortical layers. The medulla lies centrally and has chromaffin cells.
notes.D: Glomerulosa cells form small rounded groups, while fasciculata cells form radial cords separated by sinusoidal capillaries.

ana-mic-sa-d-113.why: The classical epithelial junctional complex is arranged along the apicolateral membrane where neighbouring cells meet. It includes tight junctions, adherens junctions and desmosomes in sequence.

notes.A: The apical membrane faces the lumen. The complex lies just below it at the lateral boundary between adjacent cells.
notes.B: The complex is lateral near the apex. Basal attachments such as hemidesmosomes connect cells to extracellular matrix.
notes.C: The lateral membranes of neighbouring cells meet at the apicolateral complex, which seals and mechanically links them.
notes.D: The basal membrane contacts the basal lamina. The junctional complex joins cell to cell at the apicolateral border.

ana-mic-sa-d-111.why: Microvilli increase apical surface area for exchange, whereas motile cilia move luminal contents. Efferent ductules illustrate this combination through adjacent absorptive and ciliated cell populations.

notes.A: Stratified squamous epithelium is a common adaptation to mechanical abrasion. Microvilli and cilia suggest transport-related roles.
notes.B: Microvilli enlarge the absorptive surface and beating cilia move luminal contents along or mix the local fluid.
notes.C: Urothelium adapts to substantial changes in volume through superficial cells that flatten during distension.

ana-mic-sa-d-112.why: Epithelial lateral membranes carry several cell-to-cell junctions. Near the apex, tight and adherens junctions are followed by desmosomes, while gap junctions can occur elsewhere laterally.

notes.A: Desmosomes can join adjacent cells laterally. Hemidesmosomes attach the basal cell surface to the basal lamina.
notes.B: Tight and adherens junctions are lateral, but hemidesmosomes anchor the basal surface to extracellular matrix.
notes.C: Desmosomes and tight junctions are lateral. Cilia project from the free apical surface into the lumen.
notes.D: Both junctions are present, but desmosomes and gap junctions can also lie on lateral membranes.
notes.E: Both adhesion junctions are lateral, but tight junctions and gap junctions can also occupy this border.

ana-mic-sa-d-114.why: Ion-transporting epithelia use channels, pumps and transporters to alter fluid composition. Salivary and pancreatic ducts, renal tubules and choroid plexus are specialised examples in different organs.

notes.A: Surface epidermis is mainly a keratinised protective barrier. Ion-transporting ducts associated with skin are distinct epithelial structures.
notes.B: Striated salivary ducts modify the primary secretion by transporting ions, including reabsorbing sodium and secreting potassium.
notes.C: Pancreatic duct cells secrete bicarbonate-rich fluid, which carries enzymes and helps neutralise acid in the duodenum.
notes.D: Renal tubular epithelia selectively reabsorb and secrete ions to regulate body fluid composition.
notes.E: The choroid plexus epithelium transports ions to drive water movement into cerebrospinal fluid.

ana-mic-sa-d-115.why: Epithelial surface specialisations serve distinct functions. Microvilli expand membrane area, stereocilia are elongated microvilli, and desmosomes couple neighbouring cells through their intermediate filament networks.

notes.A: Classical junctional complexes connect adjacent epithelial cells. Cell-to-matrix contacts such as hemidesmosomes occur at the basal surface.
notes.B: Stereocilia are long, actin-based microvilli, such as those found on epididymal principal cells.
notes.C: Microvilli increase the apical membrane area available for absorption, secretion or interaction with the lumen.
notes.D: Desmosomes provide strong cell-to-cell adhesion by linking cytoskeletal intermediate filaments across adjacent cells.
notes.E: The intestinal brush border consists of tightly packed actin-based microvilli rather than motile cilia.

ana-mic-sa-d-116.why: The intestinal striated border is formed by densely packed, uniform microvilli on enterocytes. These apical projections increase absorptive surface area and contain bundles of actin.

notes.A: Respiratory cilia are longer, motile projections with microtubules. They move mucus rather than forming an absorptive striated border.
notes.B: Uterine epithelium can have ciliated and secretory cells, but the classical striated border identifies intestinal absorptive epithelium.
notes.C: The proximal renal tubule has a brush border of microvilli. Stereocilia are prominent in the epididymis.
notes.D: Syncytiotrophoblast on chorionic villi has surface microvilli, which have actin cores rather than microtubular axonemes.
notes.E: Uniform microvilli cover the apical surfaces of intestinal enterocytes and collectively form the striated border.

ana-mic-sa-d-117.why: The classical junctional complex contains a tight junction, an adherens belt and a desmosome. These lateral contacts provide selective sealing and mechanical adhesion between neighbouring epithelial cells.

notes.A: The tight junction seals the apex, the adherens belt anchors actin and the desmosome anchors intermediate filaments.
notes.B: Zonula occludens is the tight junction. Together with the zonula adherens and desmosome it completes the classical complex.
notes.C: Gap junctions allow communication, while hemidesmosomes anchor to basal matrix. They are outside the classical three-part complex.
notes.D: The basal lamina is extracellular and the terminal web is cytoplasmic. Neither is a cell-to-cell junction.
notes.E: The basal lamina and hemidesmosomes belong to the basal cell–matrix interface. A gap junction serves lateral communication.

ana-mic-sa-d-118.why: Goblet cells secrete mucins in intestinal lining and in larger conducting airways. Normal gastric and gallbladder epithelia lack them, and respiratory bronchioles primarily have cuboidal and alveolar lining cells.

notes.A: The stomach has surface mucous cells, while the normal gallbladder has absorptive columnar epithelium. Neither normally has goblet cells.
notes.B: Ileum, colon and trachea have goblet cells. Respiratory bronchioles have club cells and cuboidal lining cells between alveoli.
notes.C: Large intestine and primary bronchi have goblet cells. The normal gallbladder lining has absorptive columnar cells.
notes.D: The trachea and appendix contain goblet cells. Gastric surface mucous cells and uterine secretory cells are distinct cell types.
notes.E: Jejunal and appendiceal epithelia contain goblet cells, as does the respiratory epithelium of the primary bronchi.

ana-mic-sa-d-121.why: Urothelium accommodates bladder distension, intestinal columnar epithelium absorbs and secretes, and non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium protects the oesophagus from abrasion on a moist surface.

notes.A: Urothelium stretches, intestinal enterocytes and goblet cells support absorption and secretion, and stratified squamous lining resists friction.
notes.B: Simple columnar epithelium fits the intestinal sample. Urothelium better fits a reservoir with repeated volume changes.
notes.C: Stratified cuboidal epithelium is typical of some ducts. Intestinal absorption and mucus secretion fit a columnar lining with goblet cells.
notes.D: Pseudostratified ciliated epithelium typically moves material along a surface. The absorbing and secreting sample fits intestinal epithelium.
notes.E: The bladder, small intestine and oesophagus are examples of the three environments, in the order specified in the question.

ana-mic-sa-d-122.why: Keratinised stratified squamous epithelium resists severe surface stress, simple squamous epithelium provides a thin barrier, and epithelial microvilli and cilia can support absorption and luminal movement.

notes.A: Filiform papillae resist friction, but the parietal capsule lies outside the filtration barrier and epididymal stereocilia are non-motile microvilli.
notes.B: The three linings match abrasion resistance, a short diffusion path and an epithelial surface combining microvillar absorption with ciliary movement.
notes.C: This places a ciliated transporting epithelium at the thin exchange surface and simple squamous epithelium at the absorptive motile surface.

ana-mic-sa-d-123.why: Tight junctions between surface umbrella cells seal the paracellular route in urothelium. Their apical membrane specialisations also restrict movement of urine through the cells themselves.

notes.A: Gap junctions allow ions and small molecules to pass directly between cells. They do not seal the extracellular pathway.
notes.B: Tight junctions restrict solute and water passage between adjacent umbrella cells near their apical borders.
notes.C: Desmosomes support mechanical adhesion between cells, while tight junctions provide the principal paracellular seal.
notes.D: The terminal web is a cytoskeletal network beneath an apical surface rather than an intercellular seal.
notes.E: Hemidesmosomes anchor epithelial cells to basal matrix. They do not join adjacent umbrella cells at the luminal border.

ana-mic-sa-d-127.why: Branched ducts reaching an epithelial surface identify a compound exocrine gland. Dark secretory cells with round nuclei fit a serous gland, such as the parotid.

notes.A: Endocrine products enter interstitial fluid and blood without ducts. The branched passages here indicate compound exocrine secretion.
notes.B: A branched duct system defines the compound arrangement, and the dark units with round nuclei suggest serous cells.
notes.C: The lobulated, compound serous architecture is consistent with a discrete major salivary gland, particularly the parotid.
notes.D: Serous cells usually release a watery, protein-rich secretion. In the parotid this includes digestive enzymes such as amylase.

ana-mic-sa-d-128.why: Merocrine secretion releases a vesicle’s contents by exocytosis while the cell remains intact. It is common in exocrine glands such as the salivary glands.

notes.A: Some histology texts use eccrine for the exocytotic mode. The term also names the sweat glands that use this mechanism.
notes.B: A secretory vesicle fuses with the apical membrane and releases its contents without loss of the cell apex.
notes.C: Release of membrane-bound apical cytoplasm describes apocrine secretion, as in mammary lipid release.
notes.D: Holocrine secretion involves disintegration of whole cells, as in the sebaceous glands.
notes.E: Merocrine secretion is the commonest exocrine release mechanism and is used by salivary and pancreatic acinar cells.

ana-mic-sa-d-129.why: Branched ducts and serous secretory units fit both parotid and exocrine pancreas. Ductless cell clusters closely associated with capillaries identify the endocrine islets of the pancreas.

notes.A: Both specimens have an exocrine component with serous cells organised around small lumina connected to ducts.
notes.B: Parotid tissue is serous and exocrine. Pancreas has exocrine acini and separate endocrine islets.
notes.C: The islet-like clusters identify the second specimen as pancreas. The first fits the purely exocrine parotid.
notes.D: This reverses the identification. Islets are present in the pancreas, while parotid tissue lacks an endocrine component.
notes.E: The described exocrine components have branching ducts and tubuloacinar units that secrete by exocytosis.

ana-mic-sa-e-76.why: Ciliated pseudostratified columnar epithelium with goblet cells lines much of the conducting airway. It helps humidify inspired air and moves mucus containing trapped particles toward the pharynx.

notes.A: This respiratory lining occurs in most of the nasal cavity, parts of the larynx and the secondary bronchi.
notes.B: The trachea has respiratory epithelium. The membranous urethra and vas deferens have different columnar linings.
notes.C: Primary bronchi have respiratory epithelium. Terminal bronchioles usually have a simple cuboidal or low columnar lining with club cells.
notes.D: The trachea fits, but the epididymis has stereocilia and the membranous urethra lacks the typical goblet-cell respiratory lining.
notes.E: Primary bronchi fit. The penile urethra has a different columnar lining, and respiratory bronchioles have cuboidal and alveolar regions.

ana-mic-sa-g-82.why: Gap junctions are paired connexon channels that link neighbouring cytoplasms. They allow ions and small molecules to move between cells and can coordinate electrical or metabolic activity.

notes.B: Tight junctions restrict movement through the space between cells. They do not provide a channel between their cytoplasms.
notes.C: Desmosomes connect intermediate filaments for mechanical strength. They have no channel for intercellular passage of solutes.
notes.D: The classical junctional complex includes tight and adherens junctions and desmosomes. Gap junctions are the specific intercellular channels.
notes.E: Human tissues contain gap junctions, for example in cardiac muscle where they help propagate electrical activity between cells.

ana-mic-sa-j-24.why: Oesophageal muscularis externa changes from skeletal muscle proximally through a mixed middle segment to smooth muscle distally. Mucous cardiac glands may occur in the lamina propria near the ends.

notes.A: Mucous glands can occur in the lamina propria near the ends, and the terminal muscularis externa is smooth muscle.
notes.B: The middle portion typically has a mixture of skeletal and smooth muscle. The inferior portion is predominantly smooth muscle.
notes.C: The proximal muscularis externa is skeletal muscle, with a transition to mixed muscle farther down.

ana-mic-sa-j-63.why: Centroacinar cells are the beginning of pancreatic intercalated ducts within serous acini. The exocrine pancreas has no striated ducts, which helps distinguish it from parotid tissue.

notes.A: Submandibular glands are mixed, predominantly serous, and have prominent striated ducts for modifying saliva.
notes.C: Sublingual glands have predominantly mucous secretory units. They lack the pancreatic pattern of ducts starting inside acini.
notes.D: The parotid is predominantly serous and has intercalated ducts, but striated ducts are present and centroacinar cells are absent.
notes.E: Brunner’s glands are mucous glands in the duodenal submucosa. Their secretions help protect against gastric acid.

ana-mic-sa-d-82.why: Cartilage provides flexible support, low-friction joint surfaces and a template for endochondral bone formation. Growth plate cartilage allows many long bones to increase in length.

notes.A: Hyaline cartilage forms an embryonic model that is progressively replaced by bone during endochondral ossification.
notes.B: Cartilage has a resilient extracellular matrix that gives shape and support to structures such as the nose.
notes.C: Growth plate chondrocytes proliferate and enlarge before their matrix is replaced by bone, extending the shaft.
notes.D: Smooth articular cartilage covers bony ends in synovial joints and helps distribute load with low friction.
notes.E: Cartilage rings or plates support the trachea and larger bronchi and help keep their airways open.

ana-mic-sa-d-84.why: Longitudinal growth accelerates at puberty when growth plate chondrocytes proliferate and hypertrophy. Endochondral replacement of cartilage on the metaphyseal side progressively lengthens the bone.

notes.A: The epiphysis is the bony end region. The growth plate lies between it and the metaphysis during growth.
notes.B: The epiphyseal line is the remnant after plate closure and lacks a proliferating cartilage zone.
notes.C: Dense cortical bone can grow in thickness by apposition, while longitudinal growth depends on the cartilage plate.
notes.D: The growth plate has proliferating and hypertrophic zones whose cartilage production and replacement lengthen the bone.
notes.E: Trabecular bone remodels and accumulates below the plate. The growth-related proliferation and hypertrophy occur in cartilage.

ana-mic-sa-d-86.why: Fibroblasts synthesise the fibres and glycosaminoglycan-rich ground substance of connective tissue. Reticular stromal cells are specialised fibroblast-like cells that produce supporting reticular fibres in certain organs.

notes.A: Fibroblasts make extracellular matrix. Macrophages primarily engulf material and produce signals that can regulate matrix turnover.
notes.B: Reticular cells produce stroma. Mast cells contain granules rich in substances such as histamine and heparin and are not principal matrix builders.
notes.C: Fibroblasts produce matrix broadly, and specialised reticular cells build the type III collagen networks of certain stromal tissues.
notes.D: Plasma cells secrete immunoglobulins, whereas fibroblasts and reticular stromal cells are the relevant matrix-producing populations here.
notes.E: Reticular cells also make supporting matrix in certain organs, even though they are specialised members of the fibroblast lineage.

ana-mic-sa-d-88.why: Elastic connective tissue contains abundant elastic fibres that permit stretching and recoil. Elastic fibres develop before birth and remain important in structures such as the adult ligamenta flava.

notes.A: Elastic fibres form during development and persist in adult tissues where stretch and recoil are needed.
notes.B: Adults retain elastin-rich structures, for example the ligamenta flava and elastic lamellae of large arteries.
notes.C: The umbilical cord is characterised by Wharton’s jelly, a mucous connective tissue rich in hydrated ground substance.
notes.D: Stellate cells in mucoid ground substance describe mucous connective tissue, especially in the umbilical cord.
notes.E: A jelly-like ground substance with collagen fibres is typical of mucous connective tissue. Elastic tissue has prominent elastic fibres.

ana-mic-sa-d-93.why: An osteon in compact bone has concentric lamellae around a central neurovascular canal. Osteocytes occupy lacunae between lamellae and communicate through processes running in canaliculi.

notes.A: The canal contains vessels, nerves and connective tissue. Osteocytes are embedded in lacunae in the surrounding mineralised matrix.
notes.B: Concentric lamellae form the osteon around its central canal, and osteocytes occupy lacunae between lamellae.
notes.C: Vessels lie within the canal, while bony lamellae form the surrounding cylindrical wall of the osteon.
notes.D: Canaliculi run through bone matrix between lacunae. The canal itself carries vessels and nerves.

ana-mic-sa-d-95.why: Appositional cartilage growth adds tissue at the surface. Progenitors in the inner perichondrium become chondroblasts and secrete matrix, whereas division of embedded chondrocytes expands cartilage internally.

notes.A: Clones arising inside the matrix are isogenous groups produced by interstitial growth of existing chondrocytes.
notes.B: New chondroblasts are added at the surface as well as the matrix that those cells secrete.
notes.C: The chondrogenic perichondrial layer provides cells for apposition. Division of internal chondrocytes causes interstitial growth.
notes.D: Differentiation in mesenchyme describes initial cartilage formation generally. Apposition specifically adds cartilage through perichondrial progenitors at an existing surface.

ana-mic-sa-d-97.why: The perichondrium has an outer fibrous layer and an inner chondrogenic layer. Its vessels supply nutrients by diffusion, and its inner progenitors add cartilage at the surface.

notes.A: The two layers are outer fibrous and inner chondrogenic. Cortex and medulla are not the names of these layers.
notes.B: The perichondrium provides cells for appositional growth. Interstitial growth comes from chondrocyte division within the matrix.
notes.C: Blood vessels in the perichondrium supply nutrients that diffuse into the avascular cartilage matrix.
notes.D: Progenitor cells in the inner layer differentiate into chondroblasts, which secrete new surface matrix.
notes.E: The outer perichondrial layer is fibrous and vascular. The underlying cartilage is the avascular tissue.

ana-mic-sa-d-98.why: The intervening disc of the pubic symphysis is fibrocartilage. Its thick collagen bundles and rows of chondrocytes help the joint resist tension and compression.

notes.A: Rows of chondrocytes between thick collagen bundles are characteristic of the fibrocartilaginous disc.
notes.B: Thin hyaline cartilage covers the pubic articular surfaces, but the disc itself has collagen-rich fibrocartilage.
notes.C: Fibrocartilage forms the central pad connecting the pubic bones in this secondary cartilaginous joint.
notes.D: Elastic cartilage contains a prominent elastic fibre network and is characteristic of sites such as the auricle.
notes.E: The mature symphyseal disc has abundant coarse collagen bundles and established chondrocytes in lacunae.

ana-mic-sa-d-100.why: Type III collagen forms reticular fibres that support many soft organs. It is abundant in marrow, lymph nodes, spleen and delicate stromal networks of liver, lung and kidney.

notes.A: The spleen and lymph nodes have reticular fibre networks that support the cells of their parenchyma.
notes.B: Lymph nodes have reticular stroma, but the thymic parenchyma uses an epithelial reticular framework as its main support.
notes.C: Reticular fibres support blood-forming marrow and are found among the stromal fibres of the kidney.
notes.D: Reticular fibres support hepatic plates and form part of delicate connective tissue networks in the lung.
notes.E: Kidney stroma and haematopoietic tissue both have reticular fibres made chiefly from type III collagen.

ana-mic-sa-d-101.why: Macrophages are tissue phagocytes with abundant lysosomes. Some remain resident at specialised sites, while others migrate through connective tissue to clear microbes and cellular debris.

notes.A: Some tissue macrophages remain relatively fixed in their local environment, such as Kupffer cells associated with liver sinusoids.
notes.B: Migratory macrophages can move through tissues by amoeboid movement in response to inflammatory signals.
notes.C: Alveolar macrophages phagocytose inhaled particles and microbes on the air-facing surfaces of the lung.
notes.D: Lysosomes help degrade ingested material. Kupffer cells are macrophages associated with hepatic sinusoids.
notes.E: Phagocytic uptake of appropriate vital dyes or particulate tracers can reveal macrophages in classical histology demonstrations.

ana-mic-sa-d-103.why: In interstitial growth, chondrocytes divide within existing cartilage matrix and form isogenous groups. Their secretion of additional matrix separates the daughter cells and expands the tissue internally.

notes.A: Mitosis provides new chondrocytes, and their matrix secretion increases the volume of cartilage from within.
notes.B: Perichondrial progenitors add cartilage at its surface, a mechanism known as appositional growth.
notes.C: Existing chondrocytes can divide within lacunae, leaving neighbouring daughter cells surrounded by cartilage matrix.
notes.D: An isogenous group forms from division of a single chondrocyte, so its clustered cells share a lineage.
notes.E: New matrix laid down close to lacunae contributes to the territorial matrix surrounding chondrocytes or cell groups.

ana-mic-sa-d-105.why: Abdominal aponeuroses are broad, flat tendons of dense collagenous connective tissue. Their organised fibres transmit muscle tension across the abdominal wall and contribute to structures such as the linea alba.

notes.A: Their collagen fibres are arranged in organised layers adapted to carry tension from the abdominal muscles.
notes.B: Dense irregular tissue has less consistently aligned bundles, whereas aponeurotic layers have fibres oriented along lines of muscle pull.
notes.C: Loose connective tissue contains sparser fibres and more ground substance. An aponeurosis is a dense load-transmitting sheet.
notes.D: Like cord-like tendons, aponeuroses use dense regular collagen to transmit force, but their attachments are broad and flat.
notes.E: A skeletal muscle can take origin from or insert into an aponeurosis, which passes its force to another structure.

ana-mic-sa-d-107.why: White adipose tissue is made chiefly of lipid-storing adipocytes. It serves as an energy reserve, limits heat loss and cushions sites exposed to pressure, including the soles.

notes.A: Adipose tissue is highly cellular. Its principal elements are adipocytes supported by a fine connective tissue framework.
notes.B: Adipocytes dominate the tissue. Body fat can make up about one-fifth or more of adult weight, with substantial individual variation.
notes.C: Insulation and stored metabolic fuel are normal roles. Phagocytosis is characteristic of macrophages rather than adipocytes.
notes.D: Adipocytes store triglycerides and can release fatty acids for use as fuel when energy demand rises.
notes.E: Fat pads in the soles cushion bony structures and help distribute mechanical loads during walking and standing.

ana-mic-sa-d-108.why: Brown adipocytes have many small lipid droplets and abundant mitochondria for thermogenesis. Brown fat is prominent in late fetal and newborn life and persists in variable amounts in adults.

notes.A: One large lipid droplet characterises a white adipocyte. Brown adipocytes have several droplets and many mitochondria.
notes.B: Developing fetuses and newborns have conspicuous multilocular brown adipose deposits that support heat production after birth.
notes.C: White adipose tissue is much more abundant overall. Brown adipocytes are concentrated in smaller specialised depots.
notes.D: Sympathetic noradrenergic input activates brown adipose thermogenesis, especially during cold exposure.
notes.E: Subcutaneous insulation is mainly provided by white fat. Brown fat specialises in generating heat through uncoupled respiration.

ana-mic-sa-d-110.why: A mature scar is collagen-rich connective tissue deposited by fibroblasts during repair. It replaces tissue that did not regenerate and can restore mechanical continuity.

notes.A: Epithelium can cover a healed surface, but the collagen-rich scar beneath it is connective tissue.
notes.B: Fibroblasts lay down extracellular collagen, which remodels into the dense connective tissue of a mature scar.
notes.C: Fibrosis can replace damaged muscle, but the scar consists primarily of collagen-rich connective tissue.
notes.D: Nervous tissue contains neurons and supporting cells. A typical fibrous scar is chiefly fibroblast-produced extracellular matrix.
notes.E: Different tissues can border or cover a scar. The scar proper is the collagenous connective tissue formed during repair.

ana-mic-sa-g-69.why: Elastic cartilage provides the resilient framework of the auricle. Its elastin-rich matrix bends under pressure and then recoils to maintain the outer ear’s shape.

notes.A: Areolar connective tissue supports skin and small structures but is too yielding to form the auricle’s main framework.
notes.B: Fibrocartilage contains coarse collagen bundles adapted for load bearing, as in intervertebral discs and the pubic symphysis.
notes.C: Small auricular muscles may move the ear, but the shape of the pinna is maintained by cartilage.
notes.D: Articular cartilage covers bony ends in joints. The auricle requires a flexible framework enriched in elastic fibres.

ana-mic-sa-d-131.why: Long striated fibres with peripheral nuclei identify skeletal muscle. Spindle-shaped cells with one central nucleus and no cross-striations or intercalated discs identify smooth muscle.

notes.A: The first fibre has peripheral nuclei and cross-striations, while the second shows the central nucleus and taper of smooth muscle.
notes.B: Smooth muscle cells have a central nucleus and lack cross-striations. Those features do not match the first fibre.
notes.C: Collagen is extracellular and has no nucleus. The second structure is a nucleated spindle-shaped cell.
notes.D: Cardiac myocytes usually have central nuclei and intercalated discs. Collagen cannot account for the central nucleus of the second fibre.
notes.E: The second fibre fits smooth muscle, but peripheral nuclei and multinucleation of the first fibre favour skeletal muscle.

ana-mic-sa-d-133.why: Smooth muscle is found in blood vessels and many viscera, and gap junctions can coordinate neighbouring cells. Skeletal muscle also occurs in some visceral structures, including the upper oesophagus.

notes.A: Gap junctions electrically couple many smooth muscle cells. Mechanical cell contacts can include desmosome-like junctions in some smooth muscles.
notes.B: Cardiomyocyte nuclei are usually central. Peripheral nuclei are characteristic of mature skeletal muscle fibres.
notes.C: Smooth muscle uses gap junctions for communication. Sealing tight junctions are more characteristic of epithelial barriers.
notes.D: Some visceral structures contain skeletal muscle. Examples include the upper oesophagus and parts of the pharynx.
notes.E: Smooth muscle in the tunica media of many vessels adjusts lumen diameter and contributes to vascular tone.

ana-mic-sa-g-85.why: Skeletal muscle fibres are long, parallel, striated cells formed by fusion of myoblasts. Mature fibres usually contain many nuclei arranged near the edge of the cell.

notes.A: Skeletal fibres are usually striated and under voluntary control, but a mature fibre normally has many nuclei.
notes.B: Fibres generally lie parallel within a fascicle, so their tension acts along a shared direction.
notes.C: Branching and rejoining are characteristic of cardiac muscle. Skeletal fibres are typically long, cylindrical and unbranched.
notes.D: Skeletal fibres have cross-striations and lack intercalated discs. Cardiac muscle has both striations and intercalated discs.
notes.E: The diaphragm, soft palate and tongue contain skeletal muscle. The ureter propels urine with smooth muscle.

ana-mic-sa-g-87.why: Neurons respond to stimulation and transmit signals through their specialised processes. Most have several receptive dendrites and one axon that conducts action potentials toward target cells.

notes.A: Neuronal excitability is the ability to alter membrane potential in response to stimuli and, when appropriate, generate an action potential.
notes.B: Neurons have cellular extensions called processes. These include dendrites and axons with different signalling roles.
notes.C: Most multipolar neurons have many dendrites and a single axon, although neuronal shapes differ between populations.
notes.D: Axons usually conduct action potentials away from the cell body toward synapses or other target structures.
notes.E: An axon is a neuronal process specialised for carrying signals over a distance from the cell body.
